class-7-science-nutrition-plants.ncertRef: NCERT Class 7 Science — Nutrition in Plants. The nitrogen-fixation idea is picked up again in Class 8 (Microorganisms) and Class 9 (Natural Resources).

explainers.term: What nutrition actually means in this chapter
paras: Nutrition is the whole business of taking in food and using it — not just eating. The food supplies nutrients, which are the substances a living body needs to build itself, repair damage and release energy. The five nutrient groups named in the chapter are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals, and water and roughage are added to that list as essential components of a balanced diet.

Every living thing needs nutrients, but they do not all obtain them the same way. That single question — where does the food come from — splits all organisms into two camps, and the entire chapter is organised around that split. Get this straight and the rest of the chapter is just examples.

explainers.term: Autotrophs and heterotrophs — the split the whole chapter rests on
paras: Autotrophic nutrition is making your own food from simple inorganic substances. The word is built from Greek: auto meaning self, and trophos meaning nourishment. Green plants are the classic autotrophs, because they build carbohydrate out of carbon dioxide and water. Algae are autotrophs too — they are green because they contain chlorophyll, and they photosynthesise exactly as leaves do.

Heterotrophic nutrition is depending on others for food, either directly or indirectly. Animals and most fungi are heterotrophs. Note the word indirectly: a tiger eats a deer, the deer ate grass, and the grass made the food. Trace any food chain far enough back and it ends at an autotroph, which is why plants are called producers.

A trap worth naming now: some plants are not purely autotrophic. Cuscuta makes no food at all, and the pitcher plant photosynthesises but still traps insects. Being a plant does not automatically make an organism an autotroph.

sections.h: Photosynthesis — the food-making process
paras: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants synthesise food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. The name says it: photo means light, synthesis means putting together.
bullets: The word equation CBSE expects: carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives carbohydrate plus oxygen. Write the conditions on the arrow, not as reactants — this is a common marking point.
Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves. Its job is to trap energy from sunlight; without it the reaction does not run, which is why photosynthesis happens in the green parts of a plant.
The carbohydrate first made is glucose; the plant stores the extra as starch. Starch is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen — exactly the elements available in carbon dioxide and water.
Oxygen is released as a by-product. Almost all the oxygen in the air is there because of photosynthesis, which is why the process matters far beyond the plant itself.
Leaves are called the food factories of the plant. Food made in the leaves is carried to every other part, including the roots, which is why a root can store food it never made.

sections.h: The three things a leaf needs, and how each one arrives
paras: A leaf cannot photosynthesise unless carbon dioxide, water and sunlight all reach it. Each arrives by a different route, and CBSE likes asking about the route rather than the list.
bullets: Carbon dioxide enters through stomata — tiny pores mostly on the lower surface of the leaf. Each stoma is guarded by two guard cells that open and close it, so the plant controls the exchange rather than leaving it open.

Water and minerals are absorbed from the soil by the roots, specifically by root hairs, and are carried up to the leaves through vessels running through the root and stem. These vessels form a continuous pipeline from root tip to leaf.
Sunlight is simply absorbed by the chlorophyll in the leaf. This is why leaves are broad and flat and are arranged so they shade each other as little as possible.
Large amounts of water are lost through the same stomata as vapour, so the stomata are doing two jobs at once — letting gas in and letting vapour out.

sections.h: Other modes of nutrition in plants
paras: Not every plant feeds itself. The chapter names four alternative arrangements, and the exam almost always asks for the mode plus one named example.
bullets: Parasitic — the plant takes ready-made food from another living plant. Cuscuta, called amarbel, is the standard example: a yellow tubular vine with no chlorophyll that twines around a host and draws nutrients from it. The plant it grows on is the host, and the host is harmed.

Insectivorous — the plant photosynthesises normally but traps and digests insects to obtain nitrogen, because it grows in soil poor in that nutrient. The pitcher plant is the named example: the leaf forms a pitcher with a lid, an insect entering is trapped by hairs pointing downward, and digestive juices break it down.

Saprotrophic — the organism secretes digestive juices onto dead and decaying matter, breaks it down outside the body, and then absorbs the dissolved food. Fungi such as mushrooms and bread mould feed this way, which is why they appear on damp bread, pickles and rotting wood in the rainy season.

Symbiotic — two organisms live together and both benefit. Lichens are the textbook case: an alga and a fungus living together, where the alga makes the food and the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals.

sections.h: Nitrogen, proteins and putting nutrients back into the soil
paras: Carbohydrates need only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, all of which the plant gets from carbon dioxide and water. Proteins additionally need nitrogen, and that is where the difficulty lies.
bullets: Air is rich in nitrogen, but plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly from the air. They take it from the soil, in a soluble form.
The bacterium Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants — gram, pulses, beans, peas — and converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use.

The relationship is symbiotic: Rhizobium cannot make its own food and gets it from the plant, while the plant gets usable nitrogen from the bacterium. Both benefit, which is exactly the definition of symbiosis.
Growing a crop repeatedly removes nutrients from the soil. Farmers restore them by adding manure and fertilisers, or by sowing a leguminous crop, which enriches the soil with nitrogen at no cost.

examples.t: Iodine turns a boiled leaf blue-black
examples.d: Blue-black with iodine means starch is present, so that part of the leaf photosynthesised. This is the standard starch test, and it is the evidence that food was actually made.

examples.t: A variegated leaf goes blue-black only in the green patches
examples.d: The white patches have no chlorophyll, so no starch forms there. This single experiment proves chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.

examples.t: Cuscuta twining over a shrub
examples.d: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll and makes no food. It is a parasite; the shrub carrying it is the host and is deprived of nutrients.

examples.t: Mushrooms appearing on a rotting log after rain
examples.d: Saprotrophic nutrition. The fungus secretes digestive juices onto the dead wood, digests it outside its body and absorbs the dissolved food.

examples.t: A farmer sows gram after harvesting wheat
examples.d: Gram is leguminous, so Rhizobium in its root nodules fixes atmospheric nitrogen and enriches the soil, reducing the need for nitrogen fertiliser.

mistakes: Writing that plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide, or the reverse, as an absolute. In photosynthesis the plant takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen; plants also respire, taking in oxygen, all the time.
Putting sunlight and chlorophyll on the left of the equation as reactants. They are conditions and belong on the arrow — neither is consumed.
Calling Cuscuta a saprotroph. It feeds on a living host, so it is a parasite. Saprotrophs feed on dead and decaying matter.
Saying the pitcher plant cannot photosynthesise. It is green and does photosynthesise; it traps insects for nitrogen, not for carbohydrate.
Claiming plants absorb nitrogen directly from the air. They cannot use atmospheric nitrogen; they take it from the soil, and Rhizobium is what converts it into a usable form.
Writing that the host benefits from the parasite. In parasitic nutrition only the parasite gains — the host is harmed. Mutual benefit is symbiosis, which is a different mode.

applications.h: Crop rotation and why pulses are sown between cereals
applications.d: Cereals such as wheat and rice are heavy feeders on soil nitrogen. Sowing a leguminous crop such as gram, pea or moong between cereal crops lets Rhizobium in the root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil, restoring fertility without buying fertiliser. This is why traditional Indian farming alternates cereals with pulses, and it is the practical pay-off of the symbiosis described in this chapter.

applications.h: Why deforestation is an oxygen problem as well as a tree problem
applications.d: Every green leaf is releasing oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis and absorbing carbon dioxide as a raw material. Removing large areas of forest removes that exchange at scale — less carbon dioxide taken out of the air and less oxygen put back. The chapter's process is the mechanism behind an environmental argument students meet repeatedly in later classes.

applications.h: Insectivorous plants and marshy soil
applications.d: Pitcher plants grow in soils that are waterlogged and poor in nitrogen, so the usual route of absorbing nitrogen compounds from the soil is unreliable. Trapping insects is a workaround for one missing nutrient. This explains why insectivorous plants are found in particular habitats rather than everywhere.

applications.h: Storing food in parts that never made it
applications.d: Carrots, radishes, potatoes and sweet potatoes are storage organs swollen with starch, yet none of them photosynthesised. The food was made in the leaves and transported down. This is why a plant can be dug up for food even when the edible part grew underground in the dark.

boardQuestions.q: Why are leaves called the food factories of plants?
boardQuestions.a: Leaves contain chlorophyll, which traps energy from sunlight, and they have stomata through which carbon dioxide enters. Water absorbed by the roots reaches them through vessels. Because all three requirements for photosynthesis come together in the leaf, food is manufactured there and then transported to the rest of the plant, so the leaf functions as the plant's factory.

boardQuestions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis and state where the conditions are written.
boardQuestions.a: Carbon dioxide plus water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives carbohydrate plus oxygen. Sunlight and chlorophyll are written above and below the arrow, not as reactants, because they are conditions required for the reaction and are not used up in it. Oxygen is released as a by-product, and the carbohydrate first formed is glucose, which the plant stores as starch.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between parasitic and saprotrophic nutrition, giving one example of each.
boardQuestions.a: In parasitic nutrition the organism obtains ready-made food from another living organism, which is harmed in the process; Cuscuta growing on a host shrub is an example. In saprotrophic nutrition the organism secretes digestive juices onto dead and decaying matter, digests it outside its body and then absorbs the dissolved food; a mushroom growing on a rotting log is an example. The key difference is that a parasite feeds on a living host while a saprotroph feeds on dead matter.

boardQuestions.q: How is the relationship between Rhizobium and a leguminous plant beneficial to both?
boardQuestions.a: Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can absorb and use to make proteins. Rhizobium cannot make its own food, and it obtains food from the leguminous plant. Since each organism supplies something the other cannot obtain for itself, the association benefits both and is described as symbiotic.

boardQuestions.q: A variegated leaf with green and white patches is tested with iodine after being boiled in alcohol. Describe the result and explain what it proves.
boardQuestions.a: Only the parts that were green turn blue-black with iodine; the white patches do not change colour. Blue-black with iodine indicates the presence of starch, so starch was made only where the leaf was green. The white patches lack chlorophyll, and the fact that no starch formed there while the rest of the leaf received the same sunlight, carbon dioxide and water shows that the missing factor is chlorophyll. The experiment therefore proves that chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis. Boiling in alcohol first removes the green pigment so that the colour change from iodine can be seen clearly.

boardQuestions.q: Why do farmers add manure and fertilisers to fields, and how can a crop reduce this need?
boardQuestions.a: Growing crops repeatedly removes nutrients from the soil, particularly nitrogen compounds, so the soil becomes deficient and yields fall. Farmers restore these nutrients by adding manure and fertilisers. The need can be reduced by growing leguminous crops such as gram, pea or beans, because Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil and enrich it naturally.

assertionReason.assertion: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves of a plant.
assertionReason.reason: Leaves contain chlorophyll and bear stomata through which gaseous exchange occurs.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll to trap light energy and carbon dioxide to enter the tissue, and the leaf is the organ that provides both, which is precisely why the process is concentrated there.

assertionReason.assertion: Cuscuta is an autotroph.
assertionReason.reason: Cuscuta lacks chlorophyll and obtains its food from a host plant.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. An autotroph makes its own food, and the reason states exactly why Cuscuta cannot — it has no chlorophyll and draws nutrition from a host, which makes it a parasite.

assertionReason.assertion: Leguminous plants improve the fertility of the soil.
assertionReason.reason: Rhizobium cannot make its own food and obtains it from the leguminous plant.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Fertility improves because Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen into the soil; the reason describes the bacterium’s side of the symbiosis, which is a separate fact.

assertionReason.assertion: The pitcher plant traps and digests insects.
assertionReason.reason: The pitcher plant is unable to carry out photosynthesis.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. The pitcher plant is green and does photosynthesise. It traps insects because it grows in soil deficient in nitrogen, so the insects supply nitrogen, not carbohydrate.

quiz.q: In the equation for photosynthesis, where should sunlight and chlorophyll be written?
options: With the reactants on the left
Above and below the arrow as conditions
With the products on the right
They are not shown at all
quiz.why: Sunlight and chlorophyll are conditions required for the reaction and are not consumed by it, so they are written on the arrow rather than as reactants or products.

quiz.q: A plant with yellow tubular stems, no leaves and no chlorophyll is found twining around a shrub. Its mode of nutrition is:
quiz.why: It takes ready-made food from a living host plant, which is harmed. That is parasitic nutrition — this is Cuscuta. A saprotroph would feed on dead matter instead.

quiz.q: Which organism converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form that plants can use?
quiz.why: Rhizobium is a bacterium living in the root nodules of leguminous plants; it fixes atmospheric nitrogen. Chlorophyll is a pigment, not an organism, and lichens are an alga-fungus symbiosis.

quiz.q: A leaf is tested with iodine and turns blue-black. This shows the presence of:
quiz.why: Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch. Since starch is the stored product of photosynthesis, the test is used as evidence that food was made in that part of the leaf.

quiz.q: Lichens are cited as an example of which mode of nutrition?
quiz.why: A lichen is an alga and a fungus living together, where the alga supplies food and the fungus supplies shelter, water and minerals. Both benefit, which is symbiosis.

glossary.def: The mode of taking in food by an organism and its utilisation by the body.
Components of food such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals that are needed by the body.
An organism that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances; green plants and algae are autotrophs.
An organism that depends on other organisms for food, either directly or indirectly.
The process by which green plants synthesise food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.
The green pigment present in leaves that traps energy from sunlight for photosynthesis.
Tiny pores on the surface of a leaf, each bounded by guard cells, through which gases are exchanged and water vapour escapes.
An organism that obtains food from another living organism, the host, which is harmed in the process.
The organism on which a parasite lives and from which it derives its food.
An organism that secretes digestive juices onto dead and decaying matter, digests it outside the body and absorbs the dissolved food.
An association in which two organisms live together and both derive benefit, as in lichens or Rhizobium and a legume.
A green plant that traps and digests insects to obtain nitrogen, such as the pitcher plant.
A bacterium living in the root nodules of leguminous plants that converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use.

revision: Autotroph makes its own food; heterotroph depends on others. Every food chain ends at an autotroph.
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide plus water, with sunlight and chlorophyll on the arrow, gives carbohydrate plus oxygen.
Chlorophyll traps light; stomata let carbon dioxide in; roots bring water up. All three meet in the leaf.
Glucose is made first; the plant stores the surplus as starch. Iodine turning blue-black is the test for it.
Parasite feeds on a living host and harms it — Cuscuta. Saprotroph feeds on dead matter — mushroom.
Insectivorous plants photosynthesise; they trap insects for nitrogen, not for food energy.
Symbiosis means both partners gain — lichen, and Rhizobium with a legume.
Plants cannot use nitrogen from the air. Rhizobium in root nodules converts it into a usable form, which is why legumes enrich soil.

extraFaqs.q: Do plants only take in carbon dioxide and only give out oxygen?
extraFaqs.a: No. During photosynthesis a plant takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, but plants also respire continuously, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide just as animals do. In bright sunlight photosynthesis is much faster than respiration, so the net movement is carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, which is where the common oversimplification comes from.

extraFaqs.q: Why is a pitcher plant called insectivorous if it is green?
extraFaqs.a: Being green means it has chlorophyll and does make its own carbohydrate by photosynthesis. It grows in soil that is deficient in nitrogen, and proteins cannot be built without nitrogen. Trapping and digesting insects supplies that one missing nutrient, so the plant is autotrophic for its energy needs and insectivorous only to obtain nitrogen.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a parasite and a symbiont?
extraFaqs.a: Both live in close association with another organism, but the outcome differs. A parasite benefits while the host is harmed, as when Cuscuta draws nutrients from the shrub it twines around. In symbiosis both organisms benefit, as in a lichen where the alga supplies food and the fungus supplies shelter, water and minerals. The test is simply whether the partner gains or loses.

extraFaqs.q: Why must the leaf be boiled in alcohol before the starch test?
extraFaqs.a: Boiling the leaf in alcohol removes the green chlorophyll from it. If the chlorophyll were left in place, the leaf's own green colour would mask the blue-black colour that iodine produces with starch, and the result could not be read. Decolourising the leaf first makes the colour change clearly visible.

class-8-maths-exponents-and-powers.ncertRef: NCERT Class 8 Mathematics — Exponents and Powers. Builds directly on the Class 7 chapter of the same name and is used again in Class 9 Number Systems.

explainers.term: What a negative exponent actually means
paras: In Class 7 an exponent counted repeated multiplication: 2 to the power 3 means 2 multiplied by itself three times, giving 8. That reading breaks down the moment the exponent is negative — you cannot multiply a number by itself minus three times. So the meaning has to be extended, and it is extended in the one way that keeps the existing laws working.

Look at what happens going down a column: 2 cubed is 8, 2 squared is 4, 2 to the power 1 is 2. Each step down divides by 2. Continue the pattern and 2 to the power 0 must be 1, 2 to the power minus 1 must be one half, and 2 to the power minus 2 must be one quarter. That is the definition: a to the power minus m equals 1 over a to the power m, for any non-zero a.

The single most useful consequence is that a negative exponent flips a fraction. One half to the power minus 3 is 2 cubed, which is 8. Students lose marks by writing that it is minus 8 — a negative exponent never makes the answer negative. It takes the reciprocal, and nothing else.

explainers.term: Why standard form exists
paras: Some quantities are absurdly large and some absurdly small, and both are painful to write and worse to compare. The diameter of a red blood cell and the distance to a star cannot sensibly share a page in ordinary decimal notation.

Standard form, also called scientific notation, writes any number as k times a power of 10, where k is at least 1 and less than 10. That constraint on k is not decoration — it is what makes the form unique, so two numbers can be compared by looking at their powers of 10 first and only then at k.

sections.h: The laws of exponents — the complete list
paras: These hold for any non-zero integer a and b and any integers m and n, including negative ones. That extension to negative exponents is exactly what this chapter adds to what you learnt in Class 7.
bullets: Product with the same base: a to the m times a to the n equals a to the m plus n. Add the exponents.
Quotient with the same base: a to the m divided by a to the n equals a to the m minus n. Subtract the exponents.
Power of a power: a to the m, all raised to n, equals a to the m times n. Multiply the exponents.
Same exponent, different bases: a to the m times b to the m equals a times b, all to the m.
Quotient with the same exponent: a to the m divided by b to the m equals a over b, all to the m.
Zero exponent: a to the power 0 equals 1 for every non-zero a. This follows from the quotient law, since a to the m divided by a to the m is both 1 and a to the power 0.
Negative exponent: a to the minus m equals 1 over a to the m. Equivalently, a fraction raised to a negative power is the reciprocal fraction raised to the positive power.

sections.h: Writing a number in standard form
paras: The method is the same for large and small numbers; only the sign of the power changes.
bullets: Place the decimal point immediately after the first non-zero digit. That number is k, and it will automatically satisfy 1 is less than or equal to k, which is less than 10.
Count how many places the decimal point moved. That count is the magnitude of the power of 10.
If the original number was large, so the point moved left, the power is positive. If the original number was small, so the point moved right, the power is negative.
Check by sanity: a number bigger than 1 always gets a positive power, a number smaller than 1 always gets a negative power. If your sign disagrees with that, you have made an error.
To convert back from standard form, move the decimal point the stated number of places — right for a positive power, left for a negative one — filling with zeros as needed.

sections.h: Comparing and combining numbers in standard form
paras: Standard form is not only a way of writing numbers; it is a way of comparing them quickly, and CBSE tests that.
bullets: To compare two numbers in standard form, compare the powers of 10 first. The number with the larger power is larger, regardless of k, because k is confined to the range 1 to 10.
Only if the powers are equal do you compare the values of k.
To add or subtract numbers in standard form, first rewrite them so both have the same power of 10, then add or subtract the k values and keep the common power.
After adding, the result may no longer be in standard form — if k has become 10 or more, adjust by increasing the power of 10 by one and dividing k by 10.

numericals.q: Simplify and express the result with a positive exponent: (−4)^5 ÷ (−4)^8.
steps: The bases are the same, so use the quotient law: subtract the exponents.
Apply the negative-exponent rule: (−4)^(−3) = 1 ÷ (−4)^3.
(−4)^3 = −64, so the expression equals 1 ÷ (−64).

numericals.q: Find the value of (3^0 + 4^(−1)) × 2^2.
steps: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, so 3^0 = 1.
4^(−1) = 1/4 by the negative-exponent rule.
The bracket becomes 1 + 1/4 = 5/4.
2^2 = 4, so the product is (5/4) × 4.
A fraction raised to a negative power becomes the reciprocal raised to the positive power.

numericals.q: Express 0.00000000837 in standard form.
steps: The first non-zero digit is 8, so k = 8.37.
Move the decimal point from its original position to just after the 8; it moves 9 places to the right.
The original number is smaller than 1, so the power of 10 is negative.
Therefore the number is 8.37 × 10 to the power −9.

numericals.q: Find the value of m for which (−3)^(m+1) × (−3)^5 = (−3)^7.
steps: The bases are equal, so use the product law and add the exponents on the left.
Since the bases are equal and non-zero, the exponents must be equal: m + 6 = 7.
Solve for m.

numericals.q: The size of a plant cell is 0.00001275 m and the size of a red blood cell is 0.000007 m. Which is larger, and by how many times approximately?
steps: Write both in standard form. 0.00001275 = 1.275 × 10⁻⁵ m.
0.000007 = 7 × 10⁻⁶ m, which can be rewritten as 0.7 × 10⁻⁵ m to share a power.
With the same power of 10, compare k: 1.275 against 0.7, so the plant cell is larger.
Divide: 1.275 ÷ 0.7 is approximately 1.82.
numericals.answer: The plant cell is larger, roughly 1.8 times the size of the red blood cell

examples.t: 2⁻³ is one eighth, not minus eight
examples.d: The negative sign is in the exponent, not the base. It signals a reciprocal, so 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. The answer stays positive.

examples.t: (2/5)⁻² becomes (5/2)²
examples.d: A negative exponent on a fraction flips the fraction and makes the exponent positive, giving 25/4.

examples.t: 10⁵ ÷ 10⁵ shows why a⁰ = 1
examples.d: Any number divided by itself is 1, and the quotient law gives 10⁰. Both must be the same, so 10⁰ = 1.

examples.t: 43,000,000 in standard form
examples.d: Put the point after the 4 to get 4.3, count 7 places moved left, and the number is greater than 1 so the power is positive: 4.3 × 10⁷.

mistakes: Treating a negative exponent as a negative answer. 3⁻² is 1/9, not −9. The minus sign moves the term to the denominator; it never changes the sign of the result.
Multiplying the exponents when the bases are multiplied. For a^m × a^n you ADD the exponents; you multiply them only for a power of a power, (a^m)^n.
Writing 0⁰ or applying a⁰ = 1 to a = 0. Every exponent law in this chapter is stated for a non-zero base, and 0⁰ is not defined.
Leaving k outside the range 1 to 10 in standard form. Writing 0.56 × 10⁻⁵ or 34 × 10⁶ is not standard form; k must be at least 1 and less than 10.
Getting the sign of the power backwards. A number smaller than 1 always takes a negative power; a number larger than 1 always takes a positive power.
Adding numbers in standard form without first matching the powers of 10. You cannot add the k values until both terms carry the same power.

applications.h: Reading measurements in science
applications.d: Standard form is how every quantity in physics and chemistry is written once it leaves the everyday range. The charge on an electron, the mass of a proton, the wavelength of visible light and the distance to the nearest star are all quoted as k times a power of 10, and the questions in later classes assume you can move between that form and ordinary decimals without thinking about it. The rules in this chapter are therefore not a self-contained exercise — they are the notation the rest of school science is written in.

applications.h: Comparing sizes across wildly different scales
applications.d: Standard form turns an awkward comparison into a subtraction. A bacterium at about 10⁻⁶ m and a human at about 10⁰ m differ by six powers of 10, so the human is roughly a million times larger. Once both numbers are in standard form the comparison is read off the exponents, which is far quicker and far less error-prone than counting zeros.

applications.h: Digital storage and powers of 2
applications.d: File sizes and memory are built on powers of 2, so a kilobyte is 2¹⁰ bytes and a megabyte is 2²⁰. Working out how many files of one size fit into a disk of another is exactly the quotient law — subtract the exponents. The same reasoning explains why doubling a quantity repeatedly grows it so quickly.

boardQuestions.q: State the law of exponents used when dividing two powers of the same base, and use it to simplify 7⁻³ ÷ 7⁻⁵.
boardQuestions.a: The law states that a to the power m divided by a to the power n equals a to the power m minus n, for any non-zero a. Applying it, 7⁻³ ÷ 7⁻⁵ equals 7 to the power minus 3 minus minus 5, which is 7 to the power minus 3 plus 5, that is 7². Therefore the value is 49. Note that subtracting a negative exponent increases the result, which is a frequent source of sign errors.

boardQuestions.q: Explain why a⁰ = 1 for every non-zero a.
boardQuestions.a: Consider a to the power m divided by a to the power m. Since any non-zero quantity divided by itself is 1, the value is 1. Applying the quotient law to the same expression gives a to the power m minus m, which is a to the power 0. Both expressions describe the same quantity, so a to the power 0 must equal 1. The base must be non-zero because division by zero is not defined.

boardQuestions.q: Express 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ in ordinary decimal notation and state which is larger, 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ or 9.1 × 10⁻⁵.
boardQuestions.a: For 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ the decimal point moves four places to the left, giving 0.00045. To compare the two numbers, compare the powers of 10 first: minus 4 is greater than minus 5, so 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ is the larger number. The value of k does not need to be considered here, because k is always at least 1 and less than 10, so a difference in the power of 10 always decides the comparison.

boardQuestions.q: Simplify (2⁻¹ × 3⁻¹)⁻¹ ÷ 6⁻¹, showing each law used.
boardQuestions.a: First simplify inside the bracket. Using the law that powers with the same exponent and different bases can be combined, 2⁻¹ × 3⁻¹ equals (2 × 3)⁻¹, that is 6⁻¹. The expression becomes (6⁻¹)⁻¹ ÷ 6⁻¹. Using the power of a power law, (6⁻¹)⁻¹ equals 6 to the power minus 1 times minus 1, which is 6¹, that is 6. Now divide using the quotient law: 6¹ ÷ 6⁻¹ equals 6 to the power 1 minus minus 1, which is 6², that is 36. The laws used are the same-exponent product law, the power of a power law, and the quotient law.

boardQuestions.q: The thickness of a sheet of paper is 0.0016 cm. Express this in standard form and find the total thickness of a stack of 500 such sheets, giving the answer in standard form.
boardQuestions.a: In standard form 0.0016 cm is 1.6 × 10⁻³ cm, since the first non-zero digit is 1, k is 1.6, and the decimal point moves three places to the right for a number smaller than 1. For 500 sheets the total thickness is 500 × 1.6 × 10⁻³ cm. Writing 500 as 5 × 10², the product is 5 × 1.6 × 10² × 10⁻³, which is 8 × 10⁻¹ cm. This equals 0.8 cm, which is a reasonable thickness for a stack of 500 sheets and so serves as a check on the working.

assertionReason.assertion: The value of 5⁻² is 1/25.
assertionReason.reason: A negative exponent indicates the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. By definition a to the minus m is 1 over a to the m, so 5⁻² is 1 over 5², which is 1/25.

assertionReason.assertion: The number 0.00072 written in standard form is 7.2 × 10⁻⁴.
assertionReason.reason: Standard form requires k to be at least 1 and less than 10.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. The constraint on k explains why the number is written as 7.2 rather than 72 or 0.72; it says nothing about why the power of 10 is minus 4, which comes from moving the decimal point four places.

assertionReason.assertion: For any non-zero a, a^m × a^n equals a^(mn).
assertionReason.reason: When powers of the same base are multiplied, the exponents are added.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, giving a to the m plus n, not a to the m times n. Multiplying the exponents belongs to the power of a power law.

assertionReason.assertion: The value of (2/3)⁻² is 9/4.
assertionReason.reason: A negative exponent makes the value of the expression negative.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Inverting the fraction and squaring gives (3/2)² = 9/4, so the assertion holds. A negative exponent indicates a reciprocal, never a negative result.

quiz.q: The value of (1/3)⁻² is:
quiz.why: A negative exponent on a fraction takes the reciprocal and makes the exponent positive, so (1/3)⁻² becomes 3², which is 9. The answer is positive — a negative exponent never produces a negative result.

quiz.q: Which of these is written correctly in standard form?
quiz.why: Standard form requires k to be at least 1 and less than 10. Only 4.5 satisfies that; 0.45 is too small and 45 and 450 are too large, even though all four options have the same value.

quiz.q: Simplify 2⁵ ÷ 2⁸.
quiz.why: Subtract the exponents to get 2⁻³, and a negative exponent means the reciprocal, so the value is 1/2³ = 1/8.

quiz.q: If 3^x = 1, then x equals:
quiz.why: Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1, so x must be 0. Note 3¹ = 3 and 3⁻¹ = 1/3, neither of which is 1.

quiz.q: Which number is the smallest?
quiz.why: Compare the powers of 10 first. The power −4 is the smallest of those present, and only one number carries it, so 9.8 × 10⁻⁴ is the smallest despite having the largest value of k.

glossary.def: The small raised number that tells how many times the base is used as a factor; also called the power or index.
The number that is raised to a power. In 5³ the base is 5.
An exponent less than zero; a to the minus m is defined as 1 divided by a to the m, for non-zero a.
The multiplicative inverse of a number; the reciprocal of a is 1 over a, and a negative exponent produces it.
Any non-zero number raised to the power 0 equals 1.
Writing a number as k × 10ⁿ where k is at least 1 and less than 10 and n is an integer; also called scientific notation.
For the same non-zero base, a to the m times a to the n equals a to the m plus n.
For the same non-zero base, a to the m divided by a to the n equals a to the m minus n.
Raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents: (a to the m) to the n equals a to the mn.
Writing a number using powers of 10 for each place value, for example 4032 as 4 × 10³ + 0 × 10² + 3 × 10¹ + 2 × 10⁰.
Another word for exponent; the plural is indices, and the exponent rules are often called the laws of indices.

revision: A negative exponent means reciprocal, never a negative answer: 3⁻² = 1/9.
A fraction to a negative power flips: (2/5)⁻² = (5/2)² = 25/4.
Same base multiplied — add exponents. Same base divided — subtract. Power of a power — multiply.
a⁰ = 1 for every non-zero a; 0⁰ is not defined.
Standard form is k × 10ⁿ with k at least 1 and less than 10. That range is what makes it standard.
Number bigger than 1 gives a positive power; number smaller than 1 gives a negative power. Check the sign this way every time.
To compare numbers in standard form, compare the powers of 10 first, and only then compare k.
Before adding or subtracting in standard form, make the powers of 10 equal.

extraFaqs.q: Why does a negative exponent not make the answer negative?
extraFaqs.a: The minus sign sits on the exponent, not on the base, and the exponent controls how many times the base is used as a factor rather than the sign of the result. The definition a to the minus m equals 1 over a to the m produces a reciprocal, and taking the reciprocal of a positive number leaves it positive. So 2⁻³ is 1/8. A negative result only appears if the base itself is negative, as in (−2)³ = −8.

extraFaqs.q: How do I decide whether the power of 10 is positive or negative in standard form?
extraFaqs.a: Look at the size of the original number. If it is greater than or equal to 10 the decimal point moves left and the power is positive. If it is less than 1 the point moves right and the power is negative. A number already between 1 and 10 takes the power 0. Checking against this rule catches most sign errors instantly, because a tiny number can never have a positive power.

extraFaqs.q: Is 34 × 10⁵ in standard form?
extraFaqs.a: No. The value is correct as a number, but standard form additionally requires that k lies between 1 and 10, and 34 does not. Convert it by moving the decimal point one place left in k and compensating with one more power of 10, giving 3.4 × 10⁶. The constraint on k is what makes standard form unique for each number, which is what allows two numbers to be compared by their powers.

extraFaqs.q: Do the laws of exponents still work when the exponents are negative?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, and that is the main point of the chapter. Every law you learnt in Class 7 for positive exponents continues to hold for negative integers, provided the base is non-zero. For example the quotient law gives 7⁻³ ÷ 7⁻⁵ = 7⁻³⁻⁽⁻⁵⁾ = 7², so the laws are applied exactly as before — you simply have to handle the signs of the exponents carefully.

class-11-biology-cell-the-unit-of-life.ncertRef: NCERT Class 11 Biology — Cell: The Unit of Life. Leads directly into Cell Cycle and Cell Division, and underpins Biomolecules and the whole of Plant and Human Physiology.

explainers.term: Cell theory, and the one clause that took seventeen more years
paras: Robert Hooke, in 1665, looked at a slice of cork through his own microscope and saw a honeycomb of empty compartments. He called them cells, after the small rooms of a monastery. What he actually saw were the dead cell walls left behind — not living cells at all. Anton von Leeuwenhoek was the first to observe and describe living cells.

In 1838 Matthias Schleiden concluded from his study of plants that all plants are composed of cells. In 1839 Theodor Schwann examined animal tissues, reported that animal cells have a thin outer layer now called the plasma membrane, and concluded that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and their products. Together they proposed the cell theory.

That theory had a gap: it did not explain where new cells come from. Rudolf Virchow closed it in 1855 with the statement omnis cellula-e cellula — all cells arise from pre-existing cells. The modern cell theory is therefore three clauses: all living organisms are composed of cells and their products, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Examiners very often ask specifically for Virchow's contribution, because it is the one that turns a description into an explanation.

explainers.term: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic — where the real line falls
paras: The dividing line is not size, and it is not complexity. It is whether the genetic material is enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Prokaryotes — bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO — have genetic material that is naked, not enveloped by a nuclear membrane, occupying a region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have a true nucleus bounded by a nuclear envelope.

That single difference brings others with it. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles at all: no mitochondria, no plastids, no endoplasmic reticulum, no Golgi. Their ribosomes are 70S, made of a 50S and a 30S subunit, while eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, made of 60S and 40S.

The exception worth remembering is that mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA and their own 70S ribosomes, and divide by fission. That prokaryote-like character inside a eukaryotic cell is the observation the endosymbiotic hypothesis was built to explain, and it is a favourite short-answer question.

sections.h: The prokaryotic cell in detail
paras: Bacteria occur in four basic shapes — bacillus (rod), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma-shaped) and spirillum (spiral). Beneath that variety the organisation is consistent.
bullets: The cell envelope has three layers acting as a unit: an outermost glycocalyx, then the cell wall, then the plasma membrane. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule.
Gram staining separates bacteria into two groups by how the envelope responds: those that retain the stain are Gram positive and those that do not are Gram negative.

The genetic material is a single circular DNA in the nucleoid. Many bacteria additionally carry small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA called plasmids, which confer characters such as resistance to antibiotics.

Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane. They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, and also in respiration and secretion. In cyanobacteria, membranous extensions called chromatophores contain pigments.

Bacterial flagella have three parts — filament, hook and basal body — and are thinner and structurally quite different from eukaryotic flagella. Pili and fimbriae are surface structures not involved in motility.

Ribosomes are 70S and associate with messenger RNA to form polysomes, or polyribosomes, so that several ribosomes translate the same message at once. Reserve material is stored in inclusion bodies, which lie free in the cytoplasm and are not membrane bound.

sections.h: The plasma membrane and how substances cross it
paras: The fluid mosaic model was proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972 and is the model CBSE expects you to name and describe.
bullets: Lipids are arranged as a bilayer, with the polar heads facing outwards on both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails facing inwards. This arrangement forms spontaneously because the tails are kept away from water.
Proteins are of two kinds: integral proteins, partially or totally buried in the membrane, and peripheral proteins lying on its surface.
The quasi-fluid nature of the lipid allows lateral movement within the bilayer. That fluidity is what enables growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.
Passive transport needs no energy: neutral solutes move down a concentration gradient by simple diffusion, and water moves in the same way by osmosis.

Active transport is carrier-protein mediated, moves substances against a concentration gradient and requires energy in the form of ATP. Polar molecules cannot pass the non-polar bilayer freely and need carrier proteins.

sections.h: The endomembrane system
paras: The endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles are grouped together as the endomembrane system because their functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are deliberately excluded from this grouping.
bullets: Rough endoplasmic reticulum bears ribosomes on its surface and is the site of protein synthesis and secretion; it is extensive in cells actively engaged in protein synthesis.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and is the principal site of lipid synthesis. In animal cells steroidal hormones are synthesised here.

The Golgi apparatus, discovered by Camillo Golgi in 1898, consists of flat disc-shaped cisternae stacked in parallel. It has a convex cis or forming face and a concave trans or maturing face, which are distinct in both morphology and function.

Its principal function is packaging materials for delivery within the cell or for secretion outside. Proteins arriving from the endoplasmic reticulum are modified here, and glycoproteins and glycolipids are formed.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles formed from the Golgi. They are rich in hydrolytic enzymes — lipases, proteases and carbohydrases — that are optimally active at acidic pH, which is why they are called the suicide bags of the cell.

Vacuoles are bounded by a single membrane called the tonoplast, and in plant cells may occupy up to ninety per cent of the cell volume. In Amoeba the contractile vacuole is important in excretion and osmoregulation.

sections.h: Mitochondria, plastids and the nucleus
paras: These three carry the organelle questions most often set, and the numerical details in them are precisely what the marks are given for.
bullets: Mitochondria have a double membrane. The outer membrane is smooth; the inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae which increase the surface area, and encloses the matrix. They are the sites of aerobic respiration and produce ATP, which is why they are called the power houses of the cell.

Plastids are of three kinds: chloroplasts containing chlorophyll and carotenoids, chromoplasts containing fat-soluble carotenoid pigments, and colourless leucoplasts. Leucoplasts are further named for what they store — amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts store oils and fats, aleuroplasts store proteins.

Inside a chloroplast, the space enclosed by the inner membrane is the stroma. Flattened membranous sacs called thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana, connected by stroma lamellae. Chlorophyll is in the thylakoid membranes, and the enzymes for sugar synthesis are in the stroma.
Both mitochondria and chloroplasts contain circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and divide by fission, so they are described as semi-autonomous organelles.

The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown in 1831. Its envelope consists of two membranes with a perinuclear space between them, interrupted by nuclear pores through which RNA and protein molecules move in both directions.

The nucleolus is not membrane bound and is the site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis. Chromatin exists as loosely packed, transcriptionally active euchromatin and densely packed, inactive heterochromatin.

examples.t: Mycoplasma is the smallest cell
examples.d: At about 0.3 micrometre in length, Mycoplasma is the smallest cell known. Bacteria are larger, at roughly 3 to 5 micrometres.

examples.t: The largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich
examples.d: A standard one-mark question. Note the phrasing 'isolated single cell' — the longest cells are nerve cells, which is a different superlative.

examples.t: A human red blood cell is about 7 micrometres across
examples.d: Useful as a reference scale, and it is also the standard example of a cell that has lost its nucleus at maturity.

examples.t: Centriole is 9+0, cilium is 9+2
examples.d: The centriole has nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin and no central tubule. The axoneme of a cilium or flagellum has nine peripheral doublets plus a central pair. Confusing these two arrays is the single most common error in this chapter.

mistakes: Saying prokaryotes have no genetic material or no ribosomes. They have both — the DNA is simply not enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and their ribosomes are 70S rather than 80S.
Writing that the 9+2 array is found in centrioles. Centrioles have a 9+0 cartwheel organisation; the 9+2 array belongs to the axoneme of cilia and flagella.

Including mitochondria and chloroplasts in the endomembrane system. The system is the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles only; the others are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with these.

Confusing the cis and trans faces of the Golgi. The cis or forming face is convex and receives material; the trans or maturing face is concave and dispatches it. They differ in morphology as well as function.
Calling the nucleolus a membrane-bound organelle. It is not bounded by any membrane; it is a naked region of the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is synthesised.
Attributing the whole of cell theory to Schleiden and Schwann. Their formulation could not explain the origin of new cells; Virchow supplied that in 1855.
Assuming ribosomes are membrane bound. Ribosomes have no membrane at all — they are composed of ribonucleic acid and proteins.

applications.h: Why some antibiotics harm bacteria but not us
applications.d: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S while human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, and several antibiotics act by binding specifically to the 70S ribosome and blocking bacterial protein synthesis. The structural difference described in this chapter is what gives such a drug its selective action. It also explains why antibiotics are useless against viruses, which have no ribosomes of their own at all.

applications.h: Plasmids, antibiotic resistance and genetic engineering
applications.d: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules outside the genomic DNA that confer characters such as resistance to antibiotics, and bacteria can pass them between one another. That is one route by which resistance spreads through a bacterial population. The same property makes plasmids the standard vehicle for carrying a chosen gene into a bacterial cell, which is the foundation of the biotechnology studied in Class 12.

applications.h: Lysosomes and cellular clean-up
applications.d: Lysosomal enzymes are hydrolases that work best at acidic pH and can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. This lets the cell break down worn-out organelles and material taken in from outside. If the membrane ruptures, those enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell itself, which is the reason for the name suicide bags.

applications.h: Why plant cells do not burst in pure water
applications.d: The rigid cell wall outside the plasma membrane resists the inward movement of water once the cell is full, so a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution becomes turgid rather than bursting. An animal cell without a wall has no such protection. This single structural difference explains turgidity, plasmolysis and much of the water relations work in plant physiology.

boardQuestions.q: State the three postulates of the modern cell theory and name the scientist who contributed the third.
boardQuestions.a: The postulates are that all living organisms are composed of cells and the products of cells, that the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and that all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Schleiden and Schwann proposed the first formulation in 1838 and 1839 from their studies of plants and animals respectively, but it could not explain how new cells are formed. Rudolf Virchow supplied the third postulate in 1855 with the statement omnis cellula-e cellula.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells on any four points.
boardQuestions.a: First, prokaryotes have no nuclear membrane and their genetic material lies naked in a region called the nucleoid, whereas eukaryotes have a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope. Second, prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi complex, all of which are present in eukaryotes. Third, prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits, while eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, made of 60S and 40S subunits. Fourth, prokaryotes usually possess a single circular DNA molecule and may carry plasmids, whereas eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes associated with histone proteins.

boardQuestions.q: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.
boardQuestions.a: The model was proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972. According to it the membrane consists of a bilayer of lipids in which the polar heads face the aqueous surfaces on either side and the non-polar hydrophobic tails face inward, away from water. Protein molecules are distributed in this lipid bilayer as a mosaic: integral proteins are partially or totally buried within the bilayer, while peripheral proteins lie on its surface. The lipid is quasi-fluid, so proteins and lipids can move laterally within the bilayer. This fluidity is significant because it enables cell growth, the formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division. The membrane is selectively permeable, allowing some molecules to cross by simple diffusion or osmosis without energy and moving others against a concentration gradient by active transport using ATP.

boardQuestions.q: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts called semi-autonomous organelles?
boardQuestions.a: Both organelles contain their own DNA, which is circular, and their own ribosomes, which are of the 70S type rather than the 80S type found in the surrounding eukaryotic cytoplasm. They are therefore able to synthesise some of their own proteins, and they divide by fission independently of the division of the cell. However they still depend on the nuclear genome for most of their proteins, so their independence is only partial, and they are described as semi-autonomous rather than autonomous.

boardQuestions.q: Give the structure and function of the Golgi apparatus.
boardQuestions.a: The Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898. It consists of many flat, disc-shaped sacs or cisternae, generally about half a micrometre to one micrometre in diameter, stacked parallel to one another and held together concentrically near the nucleus. The stack has two distinct faces: the convex cis or forming face and the concave trans or maturing face, which differ in morphology as well as in function. Its main function is the packaging of materials, to be delivered either to intracellular targets or secreted outside the cell. Materials to be packaged are received from the endoplasmic reticulum, modified within the cisternae, and then dispatched. The Golgi is also the site where glycoproteins and glycolipids are formed, and it is an important site for the formation of lysosomes.

boardQuestions.q: Explain why lysosomes are called suicide bags of the cell.
boardQuestions.a: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles containing a rich collection of hydrolytic enzymes — lipases, proteases and carbohydrases — which are optimally active at acidic pH and are capable of digesting carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. So long as these enzymes remain enclosed the cell is safe, but if the lysosomal membrane ruptures the enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell's own contents, destroying it. Because the organelle can thus bring about the destruction of the very cell containing it, it is called a suicide bag.

assertionReason.assertion: Mitochondria are able to synthesise some of their own proteins.
assertionReason.reason: Mitochondria possess circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion exactly. Possessing their own genetic material and their own ribosomes is precisely what allows mitochondria to carry out some protein synthesis independently, which is why they are called semi-autonomous.

assertionReason.assertion: The nucleolus is not enclosed by any membrane.
assertionReason.reason: The nucleolus is the site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Being the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis is a statement of function and says nothing about why the structure lacks a bounding membrane.

assertionReason.assertion: Ribosomes are not bounded by any membrane.
assertionReason.reason: Ribosomes occur only in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Ribosomes are composed of ribonucleic acid and proteins and have no membrane, but they occur in eukaryotes as well, and 70S ribosomes are also found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts.

assertionReason.assertion: Centrioles show a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules.
assertionReason.reason: The axoneme of a cilium has nine peripheral doublets and a central pair of microtubules.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. Centrioles have a 9+0 cartwheel arrangement with no central tubule; the 9+2 array described in the reason belongs to the axoneme of cilia and flagella, not to the centriole.

quiz.q: Which scientist proposed that all cells arise from pre-existing cells?
quiz.why: Virchow gave this explanation in 1855 as omnis cellula-e cellula, completing the cell theory. Schleiden and Schwann had proposed the earlier formulation, which could not account for the origin of new cells.

quiz.q: The smallest cell known is:
quiz.why: Mycoplasma is about 0.3 micrometre in length, smaller than bacteria at 3 to 5 micrometres. The ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell, which is the opposite superlative.

quiz.q: Ribosomes found in the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell are:
quiz.why: Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, composed of 60S and 40S subunits. The 70S type with 50S and 30S subunits is prokaryotic, and is also found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the endomembrane system?
quiz.why: The endomembrane system comprises the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with these.

quiz.q: Infoldings of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion are called:
quiz.why: Cristae are the infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane and increase its surface area. Grana and thylakoids belong to the chloroplast, and mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane in prokaryotes.

glossary.def: The principle that all living organisms are composed of cells and their products, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
The region of a prokaryotic cell in which the genetic material lies, not enclosed by any nuclear membrane.
Small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA of a bacterium, which may confer characters such as antibiotic resistance.
An infolding of the plasma membrane in a prokaryote, helping in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration and secretion.
The model of membrane structure proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972, describing proteins distributed in a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer.
Carrier-mediated movement of a substance across a membrane against its concentration gradient, requiring energy as ATP.
The endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, grouped together because their functions are coordinated.
The flat, disc-shaped membranous sacs stacked in parallel that make up the Golgi apparatus.
Infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane that increase surface area for the reactions of aerobic respiration.
Stacks of flattened thylakoid sacs inside a chloroplast; the thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll.
The ground substance enclosed by the inner membrane of a chloroplast, containing the enzymes for sugar synthesis.
Loosely packed chromatin that stains lightly and is transcriptionally active.
Densely packed chromatin that stains darkly and is transcriptionally inactive.
The core of a cilium or flagellum, containing nine peripheral doublets of microtubules and a central pair, described as the 9+2 array.

revision: Hooke saw dead cork walls and named cells; Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells; Virchow added that cells come from pre-existing cells.
The prokaryote–eukaryote line is the nuclear membrane, not size or complexity.
Prokaryote ribosomes 70S (50S + 30S); eukaryote cytoplasmic ribosomes 80S (60S + 40S).
Mitochondria and chloroplasts hold circular DNA and 70S ribosomes and divide by fission — semi-autonomous.
Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson, 1972. Polar heads out, hydrophobic tails in, proteins integral or peripheral.
Endomembrane system = ER + Golgi + lysosomes + vacuoles. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded.
Golgi: cis face convex and receiving, trans face concave and dispatching. Packaging, glycoproteins, glycolipids.
Cristae belong to mitochondria; grana and thylakoids to chloroplasts; mesosomes to prokaryotes.
Centriole is 9+0; the axoneme of cilia and flagella is 9+2.
Nucleolus has no membrane and is the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis.

extraFaqs.q: Why is Robert Hooke not credited with discovering living cells?
extraFaqs.a: Hooke examined a thin slice of cork in 1665, which is dead plant tissue. What he observed were the empty compartments left by the cell walls of cells that had already died, and he named them cells after the small rooms of a monastery. He therefore discovered and named the structure but never saw a living cell. Anton von Leeuwenhoek was the first to observe and describe living cells.

extraFaqs.q: What exactly does the S in 70S and 80S stand for?
extraFaqs.a: The S refers to the Svedberg unit, which is a measure of sedimentation rate during centrifugation rather than a measure of mass. Because sedimentation depends on shape as well as size, the values do not add in the ordinary way — this is why a 50S and a 30S subunit combine to give a 70S ribosome rather than an 80S one. The same reasoning explains why 60S and 40S subunits form an 80S ribosome.

extraFaqs.q: How is a bacterial flagellum different from a eukaryotic flagellum?
extraFaqs.a: They are different structures that happen to share a name. A bacterial flagellum is composed of three parts — filament, hook and basal body — and is very thin, with the filament being the longest portion extending from the cell surface. A eukaryotic flagellum is an extension of the plasma membrane containing an axoneme with nine peripheral doublets of microtubules and a central pair, the 9+2 arrangement, and arises from a basal body. They also differ in how they generate movement.

extraFaqs.q: Do plant cells have lysosomes and centrioles?
extraFaqs.a: Plant cells generally lack centrioles, which is why the spindle formed during their cell division is described as anastral. Their functions of storage and degradation are largely taken over by the large central vacuole, which is bounded by the tonoplast and can occupy up to ninety per cent of the cell volume. Animal cells have centrioles within a centrosome and rely on lysosomes for intracellular digestion.

class-11-physics-laws-motion.ncertRef: NCERT Class 11 Physics — Laws of Motion. Assumes the kinematics of Motion in a Straight Line and Motion in a Plane, and feeds directly into Work, Energy and Power and System of Particles.

explainers.term: Aristotle's fallacy, and why the first law was hard to discover
paras: Aristotle held that an external force is required to keep a body moving with uniform velocity. That matches everyday experience exactly: stop pushing a box and it stops. The law of motion that is actually correct contradicts daily observation, which is why it took nearly two thousand years to state.

The flaw is that the everyday case is never force-free. A moving box on a floor is opposed by friction, so the applied force is not causing the motion — it is cancelling the friction. Remove the friction and no force is needed at all.

Galileo reached this by experiment rather than argument. Rolling a ball down one inclined plane and up another, he observed that the ball rises to nearly the same height regardless of the second plane's slope. As the second plane is made less steep the ball travels further to reach that height. In the limiting case of a horizontal plane it should travel forever, which is the law of inertia.

explainers.term: Why action and reaction never cancel
paras: The third law says that to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. Students then ask, reasonably, why anything ever accelerates if every force is cancelled by an equal opposite one.

The resolution is that the two forces act on different bodies. When you push a wall, your force acts on the wall and the wall's force acts on you. Two forces can only cancel when they act on the same body, and these never do.

So when analysing motion, always fix attention on one body, draw only the forces acting on that body, and leave out the reactions it exerts on everything else. That is what a free body diagram is, and it is the single habit that makes these problems tractable. The words action and reaction are also misleading in one respect — there is no cause and effect and no time lag between them; they occur simultaneously.

sections.h: The three laws, stated precisely
paras: The marks in a board answer come from the exact wording, so learn the statements as given rather than paraphrasing them.
bullets: First law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to act otherwise. It defines the concept of inertia and identifies when a force is present — namely, whenever the state of motion changes.
Inertia is the property by which a body resists change in its state, and it is measured by mass. The three forms usually named are inertia of rest, inertia of motion and inertia of direction.

Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force, and the change takes place in the direction in which the force acts. In symbols, force equals the rate of change of momentum, which reduces to force equals mass times acceleration when the mass is constant.
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity. It is a vector, its direction is that of the velocity, and its unit is the kilogram metre per second.
The unit of force follows from the second law: one newton is the force which produces an acceleration of one metre per second squared in a body of mass one kilogram.

Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces are of the same nature, act simultaneously, and act on two different bodies, which is why they never cancel each other.

sections.h: Impulse and conservation of momentum
paras: A large force acting for a very short time is awkward to describe instant by instant, and impulse is the quantity that avoids having to.
bullets: Impulse is the product of force and the time interval for which it acts, and it equals the change in momentum produced. Its unit is the newton second, which is the same as the kilogram metre per second.
A force that acts for a short duration but produces a finite change in momentum is called an impulsive force — the blow of a bat on a ball, or a collision.

The impulse-momentum result explains why a cricketer draws the hands back while catching a ball. The change in momentum is fixed by the ball, so lengthening the time of contact reduces the average force on the hands.
Conservation of momentum follows from the second and third laws together: the total momentum of an isolated system of interacting particles is conserved. Isolated means no net external force acts.

The standard application is recoil. A gun and bullet initially at rest have zero total momentum, so after firing the momentum of the gun must be equal and opposite to that of the bullet. The gun recoils much more slowly because its mass is far greater.

sections.h: Friction — static, kinetic and rolling
paras: Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion, or the tendency to relative motion, between surfaces.
bullets: Static friction is self-adjusting: it takes whatever value is needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum. It is therefore written as less than or equal to the coefficient of static friction times the normal reaction.
That maximum value is called limiting friction, and it equals the coefficient of static friction multiplied by the normal reaction. A body begins to move the moment the applied force exceeds it.
Kinetic friction acts once sliding has begun and equals the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal reaction. It is very nearly independent of the relative speed.
The coefficient of kinetic friction is less than the coefficient of static friction. This is why a heavy object is harder to start moving than to keep moving.
Both coefficients are independent of the area of contact, which is the result students find least intuitive. They depend on the nature of the surfaces.
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which is the entire reason for the wheel and for ball bearings in machinery.

sections.h: Circular motion, level roads and banking
paras: A body in uniform circular motion has a constant speed but a continuously changing velocity, so it is accelerating and a net force must act on it, directed towards the centre.
bullets: The centripetal force needed equals mass times the square of the speed divided by the radius. It is not a new kind of force — some real force must supply it.

For a car on a level circular road, that force is supplied entirely by static friction between the tyres and the road. The maximum safe speed is therefore the square root of the coefficient of static friction times the radius times the acceleration due to gravity.
Note what the level-road result does not contain: the mass of the car cancels out. The maximum safe speed is the same for a loaded and an unloaded vehicle on the same road.
Banking the road tilts the surface so that a component of the normal reaction contributes to the centripetal force, allowing a greater speed without relying wholly on friction.

On a banked road with friction the maximum speed is the square root of the radius times g times the quantity coefficient of static friction plus the tangent of the banking angle, divided by one minus their product.

The optimum speed, at which no friction is needed at all, is the square root of the radius times g times the tangent of the banking angle. At this speed the road would be safe even if it were perfectly smooth.

numericals.q: A cricket ball of mass 150 g moving at 12 m/s is brought to rest by a fielder in 0.1 s. Find the impulse and the average force exerted on the ball.
steps: Convert the mass: 150 g = 0.15 kg. Initial velocity u = 12 m/s, final velocity v = 0.
Impulse equals the change in momentum: J = m(v − u) = 0.15 × (0 − 12) = −1.8 kg m/s.
The magnitude of the impulse is 1.8 N s, directed opposite to the ball's motion.
Average force = impulse ÷ time = 1.8 ÷ 0.1 = 18 N.
numericals.answer: Impulse 1.8 N s opposite to the motion; average force 18 N

numericals.q: A gun of mass 100 kg fires a bullet of mass 20 g with a muzzle velocity of 500 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
steps: The gun and bullet are initially at rest, so the total initial momentum of the system is zero.
No external horizontal force acts, so momentum is conserved: momentum of bullet + momentum of gun = 0.
Convert the bullet mass: 20 g = 0.02 kg. So 0.02 × 500 + 100 × v = 0.
numericals.answer: 0.1 m/s, directed opposite to the bullet

numericals.q: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a horizontal floor with coefficient of static friction 0.4. What minimum horizontal force will just set it moving? Take g = 10 m/s².
steps: On a horizontal surface with no vertical applied force, the normal reaction equals the weight: N = mg = 10 × 10 = 100 N.
Limiting friction is the maximum value static friction can reach: f = μₛN.
The block moves when the applied force just exceeds limiting friction.

numericals.q: Find the maximum speed at which a car can take a circular level road of radius 100 m if the coefficient of static friction is 0.4. Take g = 10 m/s².
steps: On a level road the centripetal force is supplied entirely by static friction, so mv²/r cannot exceed μₛmg.
The mass cancels from both sides, giving v² ≤ μₛ r g.
v = 20 m/s. Note the answer does not depend on the mass of the car.

numericals.q: Two masses of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from the two ends of a light inextensible string passing over a frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string. Take g = 10 m/s².
steps: Let the 3 kg mass move down and the 2 kg mass move up with the same magnitude of acceleration a, since the string is inextensible.
For the 3 kg mass: 3g − T = 3a. For the 2 kg mass: T − 2g = 2a.
Adding the two equations eliminates T: g(3 − 2) = 5a, so a = 10 × 1 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s².
Substitute back into T = 2(g + a) = 2 × (10 + 2) = 24 N. Checking with the other equation, T = 3(g − a) = 3 × 8 = 24 N, which agrees.

numericals.q: A force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 5 kg initially at rest. Find its acceleration and its momentum after 3 s.
steps: By the second law, a = F ÷ m = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s².
Starting from rest, v = u + at = 0 + 4 × 3 = 12 m/s.
Momentum p = mv = 5 × 12 = 60 kg m/s.
As a check, impulse = Ft = 20 × 3 = 60 N s, which equals the change in momentum as it must.

examples.t: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes
examples.d: Inertia of motion. The lower body decelerates with the bus, the upper body continues in its state of uniform motion until a force acts on it.

examples.t: A cricketer draws the hands back while catching
examples.d: The change in momentum is fixed, so increasing the contact time reduces the average force. This is the impulse-momentum relation used deliberately.

examples.t: A gun recoils when fired
examples.d: Total momentum before firing is zero, so the momentum of the gun must be equal and opposite to the bullet's. Its far greater mass makes the recoil speed small.

examples.t: It is harder to start pushing a crate than to keep it moving
examples.d: Limiting static friction exceeds kinetic friction, because the coefficient of static friction is greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction.

mistakes: Claiming action and reaction cancel each other. They act on two different bodies, and only forces acting on the same body can cancel. This is why a free body diagram must show only the forces on the chosen body.

Assuming the normal reaction always equals mg. That holds only for a horizontal surface with no vertical component of applied force. On an incline it is mg cos θ, and it changes again if the applied force is at an angle.

Treating centripetal force as an extra force to be added to a free body diagram. It is the name for the net inward force, supplied by friction, tension, gravity or the normal reaction — never an additional one.
Writing static friction as μₛN in every case. That is only the maximum value; static friction is self-adjusting and takes whatever value is needed up to that limit.
Believing friction depends on the area of contact. Both coefficients are independent of the apparent area of contact and depend on the nature of the surfaces.
Using F = ma when the mass is changing. The second law is properly stated as force equals the rate of change of momentum; F = ma is the special case for constant mass.
Forgetting that momentum is a vector. In a one-dimensional collision problem, opposite directions must be given opposite signs before applying conservation.

applications.h: Seat belts, airbags and crumple zones
applications.d: In a collision the change in the passenger's momentum is fixed by the speed of the vehicle, and nothing can alter it. What safety engineering alters is the time over which that change happens. An airbag, a crumple zone and the slight stretch of a seat belt all lengthen the contact time, and since the average force is the change in momentum divided by the time, a longer time means a smaller force on the body. This is the impulse-momentum relation applied directly to saving lives.

applications.h: Why roads at bends are banked
applications.d: On a level road the entire centripetal force must come from friction between tyres and road, which fails on a wet or worn surface. Banking tilts the road so that a component of the normal reaction points towards the centre of the curve and contributes to the centripetal force. At the optimum speed no friction is required at all, so the bend remains safe even in rain. This is why highways and railway tracks are banked at curves, with the angle chosen for the expected speed.

applications.h: Rocket propulsion
applications.d: A rocket works purely by the third law and conservation of momentum. Hot gases are expelled backwards at high speed, and the rocket gains an equal and opposite momentum forwards. It needs nothing to push against, which is why rockets work in the vacuum of space where an aircraft engine could not. The rocket's mass changes continuously as fuel burns, which is exactly the case where the second law must be used in its momentum form rather than as F = ma.

applications.h: Friction as both problem and necessity
applications.d: Friction wastes energy in machinery and wears parts out, so it is reduced by lubricants, ball bearings and polished surfaces — replacing sliding friction with the much smaller rolling friction. Yet without friction walking would be impossible, since the forward push on a person comes from the reaction to the backward push of the foot on the ground, and no vehicle could start or stop. The engineering question is never how to eliminate friction but where to increase it and where to reduce it.

boardQuestions.q: State Newton's second law of motion and derive the relation F = ma from it.
boardQuestions.a: The law states that the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force, and the change takes place in the direction in which the force acts. Momentum p equals mv, so the rate of change of momentum is the derivative of mv with respect to time. If the mass is constant it comes out of the derivative, leaving m times the derivative of v with respect to time, which is m times acceleration. Introducing the constant of proportionality and choosing the unit of force so that the constant is one, we obtain F = ma. The derivation assumes constant mass, so for a system of changing mass such as a rocket the law must be used in its momentum form.

boardQuestions.q: Why do action and reaction not cancel each other even though they are equal and opposite?
boardQuestions.a: Because the two forces act on two different bodies. For two forces to cancel and produce no acceleration they must act on the same body, and an action-reaction pair never does. When a person pushes a wall, the force of the person acts on the wall while the reaction of the wall acts on the person, so each body experiences only one of the two forces. This is also why a free body diagram must include only the forces acting on the chosen body.
