explainers.term: The three properties of charge, and why quantisation is usually ignored
paras: Charge has three basic properties that every numerical in this chapter quietly relies on. Additivity means charge is a scalar and charges add algebraically, with signs included — a system holding plus 2 and minus 5 microcoulombs has a total of minus 3. Conservation means the total charge of an isolated system remains constant; charge is never created or destroyed, only transferred.

Quantisation means charge exists only in integral multiples of a basic unit, so q equals n times e, where n is an integer and e is 1.602 times ten to the power minus nineteen coulombs. You cannot have half an electron's worth of charge.

Yet at the macroscopic scale quantisation is ignored, and the chapter says so explicitly. Because e is so tiny, a charge of one microcoulomb already involves about ten to the power thirteen electrons, and the steps between allowed values are far too small to detect. Charge is therefore treated as continuous in practical calculations, exactly as a stream of sand is treated as a fluid despite being made of grains.

explainers.term: What an electric field is for
paras: Coulomb's law gives the force between two charges directly, so why introduce a field at all? The answer is that the field separates the source from the test object. The field at a point is defined as the force per unit positive test charge placed there, so it describes what the region of space will do to any charge, without naming a second charge in advance.

The definition carries a subtlety that is regularly examined: the test charge must be vanishingly small. A real test charge would itself push the source charges around and change the very field being measured, so the field is defined as the limit of force per unit charge as the test charge approaches zero.

There is also a physical reason the field is more than a bookkeeping device. Coulomb's law as written implies an instantaneous force at a distance, whereas electromagnetic effects actually travel at the speed of light. The field carries energy and momentum and mediates the interaction, and this becomes indispensable when charges are in motion.

sections.h: Coulomb's law and the superposition principle
paras: Coulomb's law states that the force between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
bullets: In symbols, F equals one over four pi epsilon nought, times q one q two divided by r squared. The force acts along the line joining the two charges.

The constant one over four pi epsilon nought has the value 9 times ten to the power 9 newton metre squared per coulomb squared in vacuum, and epsilon nought, the permittivity of free space, is 8.854 times ten to the power minus twelve coulomb squared per newton per metre squared.
The force is repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges, and it obeys Newton's third law: the forces on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The law applies strictly to point charges at rest. For extended bodies it holds only when the separation is much greater than their size.

The superposition principle states that the force on any charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of the forces exerted by each of them individually, and that the presence of the other charges does not alter any individual pair interaction.
One coulomb is a very large unit: it is the charge which, placed at a distance of one metre from an equal charge in vacuum, experiences a repulsive force of 9 times ten to the power 9 newtons.

sections.h: Electric field and field lines
paras: The electric field at a point is the force experienced per unit positive test charge placed at that point, in the limit that the test charge tends to zero.
bullets: Its SI unit is the newton per coulomb, and it is a vector directed along the force on a positive charge.

For a point charge, the magnitude of the field at distance r is one over four pi epsilon nought times q divided by r squared, directed radially outward for a positive charge and radially inward for a negative charge.
Field lines start from positive charges and end on negative charges. If there is a single charge, the lines start or end at infinity.
Field lines never intersect. If two lines crossed, there would be two directions of the field at the point of intersection, which is impossible.
In a charge-free region field lines are continuous curves without any breaks, and electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops.
The relative closeness of the lines indicates the strength of the field: lines crowd where the field is strong and spread out where it is weak.
The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the field there.

sections.h: The electric dipole
paras: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite point charges separated by a small distance, usually written as 2a.
bullets: The electric dipole moment is the product of the magnitude of either charge and the separation, so p equals q times 2a. It is a vector whose direction is taken from the negative charge to the positive charge, and its SI unit is the coulomb metre.

On the axial line, at a distance r from the centre and for r much greater than a, the field has magnitude one over four pi epsilon nought times 2p divided by r cubed, and it points in the direction of the dipole moment.
On the equatorial line, under the same condition, the field has magnitude one over four pi epsilon nought times p divided by r cubed, and it points opposite to the dipole moment.
So the axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance, and the two are opposite in direction. This ratio of two to one is a very common one-mark question.

The dipole field falls off as the inverse cube of the distance, faster than the inverse square of a single point charge, because the fields of the two opposite charges increasingly cancel as you move away.

In a uniform external field the two forces on a dipole are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero, but they do not act along the same line and therefore produce a torque. The torque equals p cross E, of magnitude pE sin theta.
The torque tends to align the dipole with the field. In a non-uniform field the net force is not zero, so the dipole experiences both a torque and a translational force.

sections.h: Electric flux and Gauss's law
paras: Electric flux through a small area element is the product of the field, the area, and the cosine of the angle between the field and the outward normal to the area.
bullets: Its SI unit is the newton metre squared per coulomb, and it is a scalar quantity. It is proportional to the number of field lines crossing the area.
Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface equals one over epsilon nought times the total charge enclosed by that surface.
The closed surface used is called a Gaussian surface, and it is imaginary — chosen for convenience, not physically present.
Charges lying outside the Gaussian surface contribute nothing to the total flux, since every line they send in also comes out. They do, however, contribute to the field at points on the surface.

For an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire, the field is lambda divided by two pi epsilon nought r, where lambda is the linear charge density. It falls off as one over r rather than one over r squared.

For a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet the field is sigma divided by two epsilon nought, where sigma is the surface charge density. Remarkably, this does not depend on the distance from the sheet at all.
For a uniformly charged thin spherical shell, the field at an outside point is the same as if the entire charge were concentrated at the centre, while the field at any point inside the shell is zero.

numericals.q: Two point charges of 3 μC and −3 μC are placed 0.2 m apart in vacuum. Find the magnitude and nature of the force between them.
steps: Convert to SI: q₁ = 3 × 10⁻⁶ C, q₂ = 3 × 10⁻⁶ C in magnitude, r = 0.2 m.
Apply Coulomb's law: F = (9 × 10⁹) × (3 × 10⁻⁶ × 3 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.2)².
Numerator: 9 × 10⁹ × 9 × 10⁻¹² = 8.1 × 10⁻² N m².
Denominator: (0.2)² = 0.04 m². So F = 8.1 × 10⁻² ÷ 4 × 10⁻² = 2.025 N. The charges are unlike, so the force is attractive.

numericals.q: How many electrons make up a charge of −1 C?
steps: By quantisation of charge, q = ne, so n = q ÷ e.
Here the magnitude of q is 1 C and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
n = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons. The very large number is why quantisation is not noticeable at everyday scales.

numericals.q: Calculate the electric field at a point 0.3 m from a point charge of 2 × 10⁻⁶ C in vacuum.
steps: For a point charge, E = (1/4πε₀) q ÷ r².
Substitute: E = (9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.3)².
Denominator: (0.3)² = 0.09. So E = 1.8 × 10⁴ ÷ 0.09 = 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed radially outward as the charge is positive.

numericals.q: An electric dipole of moment 4 × 10⁻⁹ C m is placed in a uniform field of 5 × 10⁴ N/C at 30° to the field. Find the torque acting on it.
steps: The torque on a dipole in a uniform field has magnitude τ = pE sin θ.
Substitute p = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C m, E = 5 × 10⁴ N/C and θ = 30°, so sin θ = 0.5.
τ = 4 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.5 × 10⁴ = 1 × 10⁻⁴ N m. Note the net force on the dipole is zero because the field is uniform.

numericals.q: A point charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. What is the electric flux through the whole cube, and through one face?
steps: By Gauss's law, the total flux through any closed surface enclosing the charge is q ÷ ε₀, whatever the shape of the surface.
The cube is a closed surface enclosing q, so the total flux is q ÷ ε₀.
The charge is at the centre, so by symmetry all six faces are equivalent and each carries the same share of the flux.
Flux through one face = (q ÷ ε₀) ÷ 6 = q ÷ 6ε₀.
numericals.answer: Total flux q/ε₀; through one face q/6ε₀

numericals.q: Compare the electric field of a dipole on its axial line with that on its equatorial line at the same distance r, where r is much greater than a.
steps: Axial field: E_axial = (1/4πε₀) × 2p ÷ r³, directed along the dipole moment.
Equatorial field: E_equatorial = (1/4πε₀) × p ÷ r³, directed opposite to the dipole moment.
Taking the ratio, the factors of 1/4πε₀, p and r³ all cancel.
The ratio is therefore 2 : 1, and the two fields are antiparallel.
numericals.answer: The axial field is twice the equatorial field and points in the opposite direction

examples.t: Field inside a charged spherical shell is exactly zero
examples.d: A Gaussian sphere drawn inside encloses no charge, so by Gauss's law the flux is zero, and by symmetry the field itself must be zero everywhere inside.

examples.t: The field of an infinite charged sheet does not weaken with distance
examples.d: E = σ/2ε₀ contains no r. Moving away brings more of the sheet into view at a shallower angle, exactly compensating the increased distance.

examples.t: A charge outside a closed surface contributes zero net flux
examples.d: Every field line that enters the surface also leaves it, so the contributions cancel. It still contributes to the field at points on the surface, which is why Gauss's law is about total flux, not about E pointwise.

examples.t: A comb rubbed on dry hair picks up small pieces of paper
examples.d: The charged comb induces a dipole in each neutral piece of paper, and because the comb's field is non-uniform the induced dipole experiences a net attractive force.

mistakes: Treating charge as a vector and adding magnitudes. Charge is a scalar and adds algebraically with signs; it is the FORCE that is a vector and requires vector addition under superposition.
Forgetting to convert microcoulombs to coulombs, or centimetres to metres, before substituting into Coulomb's law. Because the distance is squared, an error in r is doubled in the answer.
Assuming the field inside a spherical shell equals the surface value. It is exactly zero everywhere inside, because the enclosed charge is zero.
Concluding that if the flux through a closed surface is zero then the field on it is zero. Zero net flux means only that the enclosed charge is zero; the field on the surface may well be non-zero.
Using the inverse-square law for a dipole field. A dipole field falls as the inverse cube of the distance, because the two opposite charges increasingly cancel.
Saying a dipole in a uniform field experiences a net force. The net force is zero and only a torque acts; a net force appears only in a non-uniform field.
Drawing electrostatic field lines as closed loops or letting them intersect. They begin on positive and end on negative charge, and crossing would give two field directions at one point.

Applying the wire and sheet formulas without checking the conditions. They are derived for an infinitely long wire and an infinite plane sheet, so they hold only near a finite object, far from its edges.

applications.h: Lightning conductors and the action of points
applications.d: Charge accumulates most densely where a conductor's surface is sharply curved, so the field just outside a pointed tip is far stronger than near a flat region. At a sharp point the field can become large enough to ionise the surrounding air, allowing charge to leak away steadily. A lightning conductor exploits this by presenting a sharp metal point to the sky, discharging the region continuously and, if a strike does occur, conducting it safely to earth.

applications.h: Electrostatic precipitators in industry
applications.d: Smoke leaving a chimney carries fine ash particles. In a precipitator the particles are given a charge as they pass through a region of strong field, and are then attracted to oppositely charged collecting plates where they stick and are periodically removed. The whole device is an application of the force on a charge in an electric field, and it is one of the main technologies for reducing particulate pollution from thermal power stations.

applications.h: Why a car is a safe place in a thunderstorm
applications.d: The field inside a closed conductor with no enclosed charge is zero, the same result obtained for the spherical shell. A metal car body approximates such an enclosure, so charge deposited by a strike resides on the outer surface and the field inside remains essentially zero. The same principle is used deliberately in electrostatic shielding, where sensitive instruments are enclosed in a metal case to keep external fields out.

applications.h: Polar molecules and why water dissolves salt
applications.d: A water molecule has a permanent dipole moment because its positive and negative charge centres do not coincide. When salt is added, these dipoles orient themselves around the sodium and chloride ions and screen the attraction between them, weakening the force holding the crystal together. The dipole in a field, and the field of a dipole, are therefore the basis of an everyday chemical fact.

boardQuestions.q: State Coulomb's law and express it in vector form. Mention two limitations.
boardQuestions.a: Coulomb's law states that the force of interaction between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and acts along the line joining them. In magnitude, F equals one over four pi epsilon nought times q one q two divided by r squared. In vector form the force on charge two due to charge one is this magnitude multiplied by the unit vector directed from charge one towards charge two, which automatically gives repulsion for like charges and attraction for unlike ones. Two limitations are that the law holds only for point charges at rest, so it cannot be applied directly to extended bodies unless their separation is much greater than their size, and that it applies to charges at rest, since moving charges also produce magnetic effects.

boardQuestions.q: Define electric field intensity. Why must the test charge be vanishingly small?
boardQuestions.a: The electric field intensity at a point is defined as the force experienced per unit positive test charge placed at that point, taken in the limit as the test charge tends to zero. Its SI unit is the newton per coulomb. The test charge must be vanishingly small because a charge of appreciable magnitude would itself exert forces on the source charges, causing them to redistribute, and the field measured would then not be the original field that was to be determined.

boardQuestions.q: State Gauss's law and use it to find the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
boardQuestions.a: Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to one over epsilon nought times the net charge enclosed by that surface. To apply it to an infinite plane sheet with uniform surface charge density sigma, choose as the Gaussian surface a cylinder whose axis is perpendicular to the sheet, with its two flat circular faces of area A lying on either side and equidistant from the sheet. By symmetry the field is perpendicular to the sheet and has the same magnitude on both faces. No flux passes through the curved surface, since the field there is parallel to the surface, so the total flux is E times A through each of the two faces, giving 2EA in all. The charge enclosed by the cylinder is sigma times A. By Gauss's law, 2EA equals sigma A divided by epsilon nought, so E equals sigma divided by 2 epsilon nought. The result is independent of the distance from the sheet, so the field is uniform on either side.

boardQuestions.q: Derive the expression for the torque on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field.
boardQuestions.a: Consider a dipole of charges plus q and minus q separated by 2a, placed in a uniform field E with its axis making an angle theta with the field. The force on the positive charge is qE in the direction of the field and on the negative charge is qE opposite to it. These forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the net force on the dipole is zero and it does not undergo translation. However they do not act along the same line, so they constitute a couple. The magnitude of the torque is one force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between their lines of action, which is 2a sin theta. Therefore the torque equals qE times 2a sin theta, that is pE sin theta, where p equals 2aq is the dipole moment. In vector form the torque is p cross E, and it acts to align the dipole with the field.

boardQuestions.q: Using Gauss's law, show that the electric field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero.
boardQuestions.a: Consider a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying charge q distributed uniformly over its surface. To find the field at a point inside, choose as the Gaussian surface a concentric sphere of radius r less than R passing through that point. By symmetry the field at every point of this surface has the same magnitude and is directed radially, so the flux through it is E times four pi r squared. The Gaussian surface lies entirely inside the shell and therefore encloses no charge at all, since all the charge resides on the outer surface of the shell. By Gauss's law the flux equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon nought, which is zero. Hence E times four pi r squared equals zero, and since the area is not zero, E must be zero at every point inside the shell.

boardQuestions.q: State any three properties of electric field lines and explain why two field lines can never intersect.
boardQuestions.a: First, field lines start from positive charges and end on negative charges, and in the case of a single charge they start or end at infinity. Second, in a charge-free region they are continuous curves without any breaks, and electrostatic field lines never form closed loops. Third, the relative closeness of the lines indicates the relative strength of the field, the lines being crowded where the field is strong. Two field lines can never intersect because the tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field there; if two lines crossed, then at the point of intersection there would be two different tangents and hence two different directions of the field at the same point, which is impossible since the field at a point has a unique direction.

assertionReason.assertion: The electric field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero.
assertionReason.reason: A Gaussian surface drawn inside the shell encloses no charge.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. All the charge lies on the shell's surface, so an internal Gaussian surface encloses nothing, the flux is zero, and by symmetry the field itself must vanish.

assertionReason.assertion: A dipole placed in a uniform electric field experiences no net force.
assertionReason.reason: The electric dipole moment is directed from the negative charge to the positive charge.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. The direction convention for the dipole moment is a definition and has no bearing on the net force. The force vanishes because the field is uniform, so the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

assertionReason.assertion: If the net electric flux through a closed surface is zero, the electric field must be zero at every point on that surface.
assertionReason.reason: Gauss's law relates the total flux through a closed surface to the charge enclosed.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. Zero net flux implies only that the enclosed charge is zero; an external charge can produce a non-zero field at every point of the surface while contributing no net flux, since whatever enters also leaves.

assertionReason.assertion: The electric field of a dipole falls off more rapidly with distance than that of a point charge.
assertionReason.reason: A dipole carries a net charge equal to twice the magnitude of either of its charges.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. A dipole consists of equal and opposite charges, so its net charge is zero, not twice either charge. The faster fall-off arises because those opposite charges cancel more completely as distance increases, giving an inverse-cube rather than inverse-square dependence.

quiz.q: The SI unit of electric dipole moment is:
quiz.why: Dipole moment is charge multiplied by separation, so its unit is the coulomb metre. N/C is the unit of electric field and N m²/C is the unit of electric flux.

quiz.q: The electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet of surface charge density σ is:
quiz.why: Applying Gauss's law to a cylindrical surface piercing the sheet gives 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/2ε₀. Notably it does not depend on the distance from the sheet.

quiz.q: At the same distance from the centre of a short dipole, the ratio of the axial field to the equatorial field is:
quiz.why: The axial field is 2p/4πε₀r³ and the equatorial field is p/4πε₀r³, so the ratio is 2 : 1. The two fields also point in opposite directions.

quiz.q: A charge q is placed at the centre of a cube. The flux through one face is:
quiz.why: The total flux through the closed cube is q/ε₀ by Gauss's law, and by symmetry the six faces share it equally, giving q/6ε₀ through each.

quiz.q: Two electric field lines can never intersect because:
options: It would imply two directions of the field at one point
quiz.why: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of the field. An intersection would give two tangents and hence two field directions at the same point, which is impossible.

glossary.def: The property that charge exists only in integral multiples of the elementary charge e, so q = ne.
The principle that the total charge of an isolated system remains constant; charge can be transferred but never created or destroyed.
The SI unit of charge; the charge which, placed 1 m from an equal charge in vacuum, experiences a repulsive force of 9 × 10⁹ N.
The constant ε₀, of value 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², appearing in Coulomb's law and Gauss's law.
The rule that the force on a charge due to several others is the vector sum of the individual forces, each unaffected by the presence of the rest.
The force per unit positive test charge at a point, in the limit that the test charge tends to zero; unit N/C.
Imaginary curves whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the field, drawn more densely where the field is stronger.
A pair of equal and opposite point charges separated by a small distance 2a.
The product of either charge and the separation, p = q × 2a, directed from the negative to the positive charge; unit C m.
The scalar quantity E ΔS cos θ, proportional to the number of field lines crossing an area; unit N m²/C.
An imaginary closed surface chosen for convenience when applying Gauss's law.
Charge per unit length, denoted λ, used for a charged wire.
Charge per unit area, denoted σ, used for a charged sheet or shell.
The use of a conducting enclosure to keep the field inside zero, since a closed conductor with no enclosed charge has no interior field.

revision: Charge is additive (scalar, with signs), conserved, and quantised as q = ne with e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Quantisation is ignored macroscopically because e is far too small for the steps to be noticed.
Coulomb's law: F = (1/4πε₀)q₁q₂/r², with 1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C², along the line joining the charges.
Superposition: forces add as vectors, and no pair interaction is altered by the other charges.
E = F/q₀ with the test charge tending to zero, so it does not disturb the source.
Field lines: start on positive, end on negative, never cross, never form closed loops, crowding shows strength.
Dipole moment p = q × 2a, directed from −q to +q, unit C m.
Axial field 2p/4πε₀r³; equatorial field p/4πε₀r³ and opposite. Axial is twice equatorial.
Dipole fields fall as 1/r³, faster than a point charge's 1/r².
Uniform field: net force on a dipole is zero, torque = pE sin θ. Non-uniform field: both force and torque.
Gauss's law: total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀. External charges add no net flux.
Wire: E = λ/2πε₀r. Infinite sheet: E = σ/2ε₀, independent of distance. Shell: outside as a point charge, inside exactly zero.

extraFaqs.q: If charge is quantised, why do we treat it as continuous in problems?
extraFaqs.a: Because the elementary charge is extremely small compared with the charges met in practice. A charge of one microcoulomb already corresponds to roughly ten to the power thirteen electronic charges, so the jump from one allowed value to the next is utterly negligible on that scale. Treating charge as continuous is therefore an excellent approximation at the macroscopic level, in the same way that a stream of sand can be treated as a fluid even though it is made of discrete grains. Quantisation matters only when the number of charges involved is small.

extraFaqs.q: Does Gauss's law mean charges outside a closed surface have no effect?
extraFaqs.a: It means they make no contribution to the net flux through that surface, which is not the same thing. Every field line from an external charge that enters the closed surface must also leave it, so the inward and outward contributions cancel exactly. However, that external charge does contribute to the electric field at individual points on the surface. This is why Gauss's law is a statement about the total flux and the enclosed charge only, and why it can be used to find E only when symmetry guarantees that E is constant over the chosen surface.

extraFaqs.q: Why does the field of an infinite sheet not decrease with distance?
extraFaqs.a: Because moving further away brings a larger portion of the sheet into effective view. The contribution of each small element does weaken with distance as expected, but the number of elements at a comparable distance grows in exactly the compensating proportion, and the components parallel to the sheet cancel by symmetry. The two effects balance precisely for an infinite sheet, leaving E equal to sigma over two epsilon nought everywhere. For a real finite sheet the result holds only close to the sheet and far from its edges, where it looks effectively infinite.

extraFaqs.q: Why does a dipole field fall off faster than a point charge field?
extraFaqs.a: A dipole is made of two equal and opposite charges. At a point far away, the fields of the two charges are almost equal in magnitude but nearly opposite in direction, so they very nearly cancel. What survives is the small difference arising from their slightly different distances, and that difference shrinks faster than either field individually. Working this out gives a dependence on one over r cubed rather than one over r squared. The same reasoning explains why a neutral object with separated charge still produces a field at all, but only a weak and rapidly diminishing one.

class-11-chemistry-structure-of-atom.ncertRef: NCERT Class 11 Chemistry — Structure of Atom. It supplies the quantum numbers and electronic configurations used in Classification of Elements and Periodicity and in Chemical Bonding.

explainers.term: Why Rutherford's model had to be abandoned
paras: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment was decisive about where the mass and positive charge sit. Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil undeflected, showing that the atom is largely empty space. A small fraction were deflected through small angles, and about one in twenty thousand was deflected through more than ninety degrees or bounced straight back, showing that all the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus. The nucleus has a radius of about ten to the power minus fifteen metres against an atomic radius of about ten to the power minus ten metres.

The model that followed — electrons revolving around this nucleus like planets round the sun — then ran into a fatal objection from classical electrodynamics. A charged particle moving in a circular path is accelerating, and an accelerating charge must continuously radiate energy. Losing energy, the electron would spiral inwards and collapse into the nucleus in a fraction of a second.

So the model predicted that no atom could exist, which is plainly wrong. It also predicted a continuous spectrum as the electron spiralled through every possible energy, whereas real atoms give sharp line spectra. Both failures point the same way: the energy of an electron in an atom cannot take arbitrary values.

explainers.term: From Bohr's orbits to quantum-mechanical orbitals
paras: Bohr fixed the stability problem by decree. He postulated that the electron revolves only in certain permitted orbits of fixed energy, called stationary states, in which it does not radiate; energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between them, with the frequency given by the energy difference divided by Planck's constant. The permitted orbits are those in which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of h over two pi.

That worked beautifully for hydrogen and explained its line spectrum quantitatively, but it failed for every atom with more than one electron, could not account for the fine structure of spectral lines, the splitting in a magnetic field or an electric field, and said nothing about chemical bonding.

The deeper problem is that Bohr's model keeps the idea of a definite path. De Broglie's proposal that matter has wave character, and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, together make a precise orbit meaningless — you cannot know position and momentum simultaneously with arbitrary precision. The quantum mechanical model therefore replaces the orbit with an orbital: a region of space where the probability of finding the electron is high, obtained from the square of the wave function.

sections.h: The subatomic particles and how each was found
paras: Each particle is associated with a specific experiment, and examiners ask for the pairing.
bullets: The electron came from cathode ray discharge tube experiments. J. J. Thomson determined the charge to mass ratio of the electron as 1.758820 times ten to the power eleven coulomb per kilogram.

Millikan's oil drop experiment established the charge on the electron as 1.6 times ten to the power minus nineteen coulomb in magnitude. Combining this with Thomson's ratio gives the mass of the electron as about 9.1094 times ten to the power minus thirty-one kilogram.

The proton was identified from canal rays, or anode rays, observed by Goldstein. It carries a charge equal and opposite to that of the electron and has a mass of about 1.67262 times ten to the power minus twenty-seven kilogram.

The neutron was discovered by Chadwick in 1932 by bombarding a thin sheet of beryllium with alpha particles. It is electrically neutral and has a mass of about 1.67493 times ten to the power minus twenty-seven kilogram, very slightly greater than that of the proton.
Atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus, and in a neutral atom it equals the number of electrons. Mass number A is the sum of protons and neutrons.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, so they differ in the number of neutrons. Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

sections.h: Quantum theory, the photoelectric effect and atomic spectra
paras: Three experimental results forced the abandonment of classical physics for atoms, and all three appear as short-answer questions.
bullets: Planck proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed not continuously but in discrete packets called quanta, with the energy of one quantum given by E equals h nu, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 times ten to the power minus thirty-four joule second.

In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency falls on it. There is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light, and the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons depends on the frequency, not the intensity. Intensity affects only the number of electrons.

Einstein explained this in 1905 by treating light as a stream of photons: the photon energy h nu is used partly to overcome the work function of the metal and the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron. The work function equals h times the threshold frequency.

The hydrogen emission spectrum consists of discrete lines grouped into series. The Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet and ends at n equal to 1; the Balmer series lies in the visible and ends at n equal to 2; the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series lie in the infrared and end at n equal to 3, 4 and 5 respectively.
The wave number of any line is given by the Rydberg expression, 109677 times the quantity one over n one squared minus one over n two squared, in reciprocal centimetres.

sections.h: Bohr's model — postulates and results
paras: Learn the three postulates as statements, and the two formulae for hydrogen as results.
bullets: First postulate: the electron revolves round the nucleus in certain permitted circular orbits of fixed radius and energy, called stationary states or orbits, and while in them it does not radiate energy.

Second postulate: energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron moves from one stationary state to another, and the frequency of the radiation is the energy difference divided by Planck's constant.
Third postulate: the angular momentum of the electron is quantised, being an integral multiple of h divided by two pi.
For hydrogen, the radius of the nth orbit is 52.9 times n squared picometres, so the orbits get rapidly further apart.
The energy of the electron in the nth orbit is minus 2.18 times ten to the power minus eighteen joule divided by n squared, which is minus 13.6 divided by n squared electron volts.
The energy is negative because it is measured relative to a free electron at rest at infinite distance, which is assigned zero. A more negative value therefore means a more tightly bound electron.

Limitations: the model fails for atoms with more than one electron, cannot explain the fine structure of spectral lines, cannot explain the splitting of lines in magnetic or electric fields, and offers no account of chemical bonding.

sections.h: Quantum numbers and the rules for filling orbitals
paras: Four quantum numbers specify an electron completely, and three rules determine the order in which orbitals fill.
bullets: The principal quantum number n takes values 1, 2, 3 and so on. It identifies the shell and largely determines the size and the energy.
The azimuthal quantum number l takes values from 0 to n minus 1. It identifies the subshell and determines the shape: l equal to 0, 1, 2 and 3 correspond to s, p, d and f respectively.
The magnetic quantum number m sub l takes values from minus l to plus l including zero, giving 2l plus 1 values. It specifies the orientation of the orbital in space.
The spin quantum number m sub s takes only the values plus one half and minus one half.
The number of orbitals in a shell is n squared, and the maximum number of electrons it can hold is 2n squared.

The Aufbau principle states that orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy. The order is given by the n plus l rule: the subshell with the lower value of n plus l fills first, and when two subshells have the same n plus l value, the one with the lower n fills first. This is why 4s fills before 3d.

The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers, so an orbital can hold at most two electrons and they must have opposite spins.

Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that pairing of electrons in the orbitals of a subshell does not take place until each orbital of that subshell has one electron, and all such singly occupied orbitals have electrons with parallel spin.
Chromium and copper are the standard exceptions, having configurations ending 3d⁵4s¹ and 3d¹⁰4s¹ respectively, because exactly half-filled and completely filled subshells have extra stability.

numericals.q: Calculate the energy and the radius of the third orbit of the hydrogen atom.
steps: For hydrogen the energy of the nth orbit is Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV.
The radius of the nth orbit is rₙ = 52.9 n² pm.

numericals.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 2.19 × 10⁶ m/s. Take the mass of the electron as 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
steps: The de Broglie relation is λ = h ÷ mv.
Compute the denominator: mv = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.19 × 10⁶ = 1.995 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s.
λ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, that is 332 pm — comparable to atomic dimensions, which is why electron wave behaviour matters in atoms.

numericals.q: How many orbitals and how many electrons are possible in the shell with n = 3? List the subshells.
steps: For n = 3, the azimuthal quantum number l can take values 0, 1 and 2, giving the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells.
The number of orbitals in a subshell is 2l + 1: 3s has 1, 3p has 3 and 3d has 5.
Total orbitals = 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, which agrees with the formula n² = 3² = 9.
Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons, so the maximum is 18, agreeing with 2n² = 2 × 9.
numericals.answer: 9 orbitals (3s, 3p, 3d) holding a maximum of 18 electrons

numericals.q: Find the number of radial nodes, angular nodes and total nodes in a 3p orbital.
steps: For a 3p orbital, n = 3 and l = 1.
Angular nodes equal l, so there is 1 angular node.
Radial nodes equal n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.
Total nodes equal n − 1 = 2, which checks against the sum 1 + 1 = 2.
numericals.answer: 1 radial node, 1 angular node, 2 nodes in total

numericals.q: Calculate the energy released when an electron in a hydrogen atom falls from n = 3 to n = 2.
steps: Energy of each level: E₂ = −13.6/4 = −3.40 eV and E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV.
Energy released = E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV.
This transition ends at n = 2, so it belongs to the Balmer series and lies in the visible region, at about 656 nm.
numericals.answer: 1.89 eV, a visible Balmer line at about 656 nm

numericals.q: Write the electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) and explain why it is an exception to the expected filling.
steps: Filling in the order given by the n + l rule up to 24 electrons would predict [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
The observed configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.
One 4s electron is promoted to 3d because the 4s and 3d energies are very close in this region.

The promotion produces an exactly half-filled 3d subshell together with a half-filled 4s, and half-filled subshells have extra stability arising from symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy.
numericals.answer: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, adopted for the extra stability of the half-filled 3d subshell

examples.t: 4s fills before 3d
examples.d: By the n + l rule, 4s has n + l = 4 + 0 = 4 while 3d has 3 + 2 = 5. The lower sum fills first, which is why potassium and calcium put electrons into 4s.

examples.t: 3d and 4p both have n + l = 5
examples.d: When the sums are equal, the subshell with the lower n fills first, so 3d fills before 4p.

examples.t: Nitrogen is 1s² 2s² 2p³ with three unpaired electrons
examples.d: By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy the three separate 2p orbitals with parallel spins rather than pairing up in one.

examples.t: Isotopes of hydrogen
examples.d: Protium, deuterium and tritium all have Z = 1 but mass numbers 1, 2 and 3, so they differ only in neutron number — the defining feature of isotopes.

mistakes: Saying an electron's energy is negative because the electron has negative charge. The sign comes from choosing zero energy for a free electron at rest at infinity; a bound electron has less energy than that, so the value is negative.
Treating an orbital as an orbit. An orbit is a definite path, which the uncertainty principle rules out; an orbital is a region of high probability, obtained from the square of the wave function.
Writing l values up to n instead of n − 1. For n = 3, l can be 0, 1 or 2 only, so there is no 3f subshell.
Applying Bohr's energy formula to multi-electron atoms. The expression with −13.6/n² is for hydrogen and hydrogen-like species only; Bohr's model fails once there is more than one electron.
Ignoring Hund's rule and pairing electrons in the first orbital of a subshell. Each orbital of the subshell must receive one electron with parallel spin before any pairing begins.
Writing chromium as [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². The observed configuration is 3d⁵ 4s¹, because exactly half-filled subshells are extra stable; copper is similarly 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
Claiming intensity of light determines the kinetic energy of photoelectrons. Frequency determines the kinetic energy; intensity determines only the number of electrons ejected.
Confusing isotopes with isobars. Isotopes share the atomic number and differ in mass number; isobars share the mass number and differ in atomic number.

applications.h: Flame tests and the colours of fireworks
applications.d: Heating a metal salt promotes electrons to higher energy levels, and when they fall back the energy difference is emitted as light of a definite frequency. Because the level spacings differ from element to element, each gives a characteristic colour — the basis of the flame test used to identify sodium, potassium, calcium and copper salts in the laboratory, and of the colours chosen in fireworks. The line spectrum is effectively a fingerprint, which is also how elements are identified in the light of distant stars.

applications.h: Why the periodic table has the shape it does
applications.d: The lengths of the periods follow directly from the number of orbitals available: two electrons for an s subshell, six for p, ten for d and fourteen for f. Combined with the n plus l filling order this produces periods of 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements, and it explains why the d block appears only from the fourth period and the f block only from the sixth. The block an element belongs to is simply the subshell its last electron enters.

applications.h: Electron microscopes and de Broglie's relation
applications.d: An optical microscope cannot resolve detail smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Since the de Broglie wavelength of a particle is Planck's constant divided by its momentum, electrons accelerated to high speed have wavelengths thousands of times shorter than visible light. An electron microscope exploits exactly this to image objects far below the optical limit, which makes the wave nature of matter a working engineering principle rather than an abstraction.

applications.h: Photocells and the photoelectric effect
applications.d: A photocell uses a metal with a low work function so that ordinary light exceeds its threshold frequency and ejects electrons, producing a current that stops the moment the light is blocked. This is the operating principle behind automatic doors, burglar alarms and light meters. It also illustrates why intensity alone is not enough: light below the threshold frequency produces no current however bright it is, which is exactly the observation classical wave theory could not explain.

boardQuestions.q: Describe Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment and the conclusions drawn from it.
boardQuestions.a: A beam of fast-moving alpha particles was directed at a very thin gold foil, and the scattered particles were detected on a fluorescent screen. Three observations were made. Most of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil undeflected, from which it was concluded that most of the space inside the atom is empty. A small fraction were deflected through small angles, indicating the presence of a concentrated positive charge that repelled them. A very small number, about one in twenty thousand, were deflected through large angles or bounced straight back, which could only happen if all the positive charge and nearly all the mass of the atom were concentrated in an extremely small volume. Rutherford therefore proposed the nuclear model, in which a tiny dense positively charged nucleus of radius about ten to the power minus fifteen metres lies at the centre of an atom of radius about ten to the power minus ten metres, with electrons revolving around it.

boardQuestions.q: What were the two main drawbacks of Rutherford's model of the atom?
boardQuestions.a: First, it could not explain the stability of the atom. An electron revolving in a circular orbit is continuously accelerating, and according to classical electromagnetic theory an accelerating charged particle must radiate energy continuously; losing energy, the electron would follow a spiral path and fall into the nucleus almost instantly, so no atom could survive. Second, the model said nothing about the distribution of electrons around the nucleus or their energies, and so could not explain why atoms give discrete line spectra rather than the continuous spectrum the spiralling electron would produce.

boardQuestions.q: State the postulates of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom.
boardQuestions.a: First, the electron revolves round the nucleus in certain selected circular paths of fixed radius and energy, called stationary states or orbits, and while revolving in these orbits it does not radiate energy, which resolves the stability problem. Second, energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron makes a transition from one stationary state to another, and the frequency of the radiation absorbed or emitted equals the difference in energy between the two states divided by Planck's constant. Third, the angular momentum of the electron in a permitted orbit is quantised, being an integral multiple of h divided by two pi, and only those orbits satisfying this condition are allowed.

boardQuestions.q: State and explain the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.
boardQuestions.a: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. Since an orbital is specified by n, l and m sub l, two electrons occupying the same orbital must differ in the spin quantum number, which can take only two values. It follows that an orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons and that these must have opposite spins. Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that pairing of electrons in the orbitals belonging to the same subshell does not take place until each orbital of that subshell has been singly occupied, and that all the singly occupied orbitals have electrons with parallel spins. This is why nitrogen, with three 2p electrons, has them in three different 2p orbitals with parallel spins and therefore has three unpaired electrons.

boardQuestions.q: Explain why the electronic configuration of chromium is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
boardQuestions.a: In the region of the periodic table where chromium lies, the energies of the 3d and 4s subshells are very close together, so the energy cost of moving an electron from 4s to 3d is small. The configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ gives an exactly half-filled 3d subshell along with a half-filled 4s orbital. Exactly half-filled and completely filled subshells possess extra stability, which arises from the symmetrical distribution of electron density and from the greater exchange energy available when a larger number of electrons have parallel spins. The gain in stability outweighs the small promotion energy, so the observed configuration is the half-filled one. Copper is an analogous case, adopting [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ for the stability of a completely filled 3d subshell.

boardQuestions.q: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and explain its significance for the concept of an orbit.
boardQuestions.a: The principle states that it is impossible to determine simultaneously and with arbitrary precision both the position and the momentum of a microscopic particle such as an electron; the product of the uncertainties in position and momentum is at least h divided by four pi. The significance is that the very idea of a definite orbit becomes meaningless for an electron, because specifying an orbit would require knowing both the exact position and the exact momentum of the electron at each instant. This is why Bohr's picture of fixed circular paths had to be abandoned, and why the quantum mechanical model speaks instead of an orbital, meaning a region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is high.

assertionReason.assertion: The concept of a definite orbit for an electron is not acceptable.
assertionReason.reason: The position and momentum of an electron cannot be determined simultaneously with arbitrary precision.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Specifying an orbit requires exact position and momentum at every instant, which Heisenberg's uncertainty principle forbids, so the orbit is replaced by the orbital.

assertionReason.assertion: The 4s orbital is filled before the 3d orbital.
assertionReason.reason: An orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons, and these must have opposite spins.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. The capacity of an orbital follows from the Pauli exclusion principle and governs how many electrons fit, not the order in which subshells fill. The order follows the n plus l rule, and 4s has the lower value.

assertionReason.assertion: The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom is negative.
assertionReason.reason: The electron carries a negative charge.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false as an explanation. The negative sign arises from taking the energy of a free electron at rest at infinite separation as zero; a bound electron has lower energy than this reference, not from the sign of its charge.

assertionReason.assertion: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of the incident light increases the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.
assertionReason.reason: Intensity determines the number of photons striking the surface per second.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. Intensity governs how many electrons are ejected, while the kinetic energy of each electron is determined by the frequency of the light through the relation involving the work function.

quiz.q: The neutron was discovered by:
quiz.why: Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding a thin sheet of beryllium with alpha particles. Thomson found the charge to mass ratio of the electron and Millikan its charge.

quiz.q: For n = 4, the permitted values of the azimuthal quantum number l are:
quiz.why: The azimuthal quantum number runs from 0 to n − 1, so for n = 4 it takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3, corresponding to the 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f subshells.

quiz.q: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a shell with n = 4 is:
quiz.why: The maximum is 2n², which for n = 4 gives 2 × 16 = 32. The number of orbitals is n² = 16, each holding two electrons.

quiz.q: The number of radial nodes in a 3s orbital is:
quiz.why: Radial nodes equal n − l − 1. For 3s, n = 3 and l = 0, so there are 3 − 0 − 1 = 2 radial nodes. There are no angular nodes because l = 0.

quiz.q: Which series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the visible region?
quiz.why: The Balmer series, whose transitions end at n = 2, lies in the visible region. The Lyman series is ultraviolet and the Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series are infrared.

glossary.def: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; equal to the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Atoms having the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
The smallest discrete packet of energy that can be emitted or absorbed, of magnitude hν.
The constant h, of value 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, relating the energy of a quantum to its frequency.
The minimum energy required to eject an electron from a metal surface, equal to h times the threshold frequency.
The minimum frequency of incident light below which no photoelectric emission occurs, however intense the light.
One of the permitted orbits in Bohr's model in which an electron may revolve without radiating energy.
A region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high; the square of the wave function gives the probability density.
n, which identifies the shell and largely determines the size and energy of the orbital.
l, running from 0 to n − 1, which identifies the subshell and determines the shape of the orbital.
m sub l, running from −l to +l, which specifies the orientation of the orbital in space.

revision: Electron: cathode rays, Thomson's e/m and Millikan's charge. Proton: canal rays, Goldstein. Neutron: Chadwick, 1932, beryllium plus alpha particles.
Rutherford: most particles undeflected means empty space; about 1 in 20,000 bounced back means a tiny dense nucleus.
Rutherford's model failed on stability — an accelerating electron would radiate and spiral in — and on line spectra.
Bohr: fixed stationary orbits, transitions give ΔE = hν, angular momentum quantised as nh/2π.
Hydrogen: rₙ = 52.9 n² pm and Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. The sign comes from the zero chosen at infinity, not the electron's charge.
Bohr fails for multi-electron atoms, fine structure, magnetic and electric splitting, and bonding.
Series: Lyman UV (n₁ = 1), Balmer visible (n₁ = 2), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund infrared (n₁ = 3, 4, 5).
Photoelectric effect: frequency sets the kinetic energy, intensity sets the number of electrons.
de Broglie λ = h/mv; Heisenberg forbids simultaneous exact position and momentum, which kills the orbit.

n + l rule: lower sum first, and on a tie the lower n first — hence 4s before 3d, and 3d before 4p.
