Nodes: radial = n − l − 1, angular = l, total = n − 1.

extraFaqs.q: Why is the energy of an electron in an atom taken as negative?
extraFaqs.a: The zero of energy is fixed by convention at a free electron at rest infinitely far from the nucleus, where there is no interaction between them. An electron bound in an atom is attracted by the nucleus and has less energy than this reference state, so its energy comes out negative. The sign therefore expresses that work must be done to remove the electron, and a more negative value means a more tightly bound electron. It has nothing to do with the electron carrying a negative charge, which is a common misreading.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between an orbit and an orbital?
extraFaqs.a: An orbit is a definite circular path of fixed radius, as in Bohr's model, in which the electron is imagined to move like a planet. An orbital is a three-dimensional region around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is high, obtained from the square of the wave function in the quantum mechanical model. The change was forced by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which makes a precise path meaningless, and by de Broglie's demonstration that the electron has wave character. An orbit can hold any number of electrons in principle, whereas an orbital holds at most two, with opposite spins.

extraFaqs.q: Why does the 4s subshell fill before 3d even though its principal quantum number is higher?
extraFaqs.a: Because the order of filling depends on the total energy of the subshell rather than on n alone, and this is captured by the n plus l rule. For 4s the sum is 4 plus 0, which is 4, while for 3d it is 3 plus 2, which is 5. The lower sum corresponds to the lower energy, so 4s is filled first, which is why potassium and calcium place their outermost electrons in 4s before the d block begins. When two subshells have the same n plus l value, such as 3d and 4p which both give 5, the one with the lower n is filled first.

extraFaqs.q: Why could classical physics not explain the photoelectric effect?
extraFaqs.a: Classical wave theory predicts that the energy delivered to an electron should depend on the intensity of the light and that a weak beam should eventually eject electrons if given enough time. Experiment shows the opposite: below a threshold frequency no electrons are emitted however intense the light or however long it shines, and above it emission is immediate with the kinetic energy depending on frequency rather than intensity. Einstein resolved this by treating light as a stream of photons each carrying energy hν, so one photon interacts with one electron and must individually carry enough energy to overcome the work function.

class-10-science-life-processes.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science — Life Processes. It is the longest chapter in the Biology section and connects to Control and Coordination and to How do Organisms Reproduce.

explainers.term: What counts as a life process, and why there are four
paras: The processes that together perform maintenance of the body are called life processes. The chapter takes four of them: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion. Each answers one question about keeping a body running — where the raw material comes from, how energy is released from it, how it is moved to where it is needed, and how the waste is removed.

The order is not arbitrary. Food taken in during nutrition is broken down in respiration to release energy; both the food and the oxygen have to be carried to every cell by transportation; and the by-products of those reactions must be removed by excretion. Losing that thread is why the chapter feels like a list of diagrams to memorise when it is really one continuous argument.

A point worth noticing early: multicellular organisms need transport systems precisely because they are large. In a single-celled organism the whole body surface is in contact with the environment, so diffusion is enough. Once the body is many cells thick, the cells in the interior cannot exchange material with the outside directly, and specialised tissues become necessary.

explainers.term: Why the human heart has four chambers
paras: The heart is a muscular organ divided into four chambers: the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle. Oxygenated blood arrives from the lungs at the left atrium, passes to the left ventricle and is pumped out to the body. Deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and is pumped to the lungs.

The point of the division is to keep the two streams separate. Mixing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood would lower the efficiency of oxygen supply, and birds and mammals need a high and steady supply because they use energy to maintain their body temperature. Animals that do not maintain a constant body temperature can tolerate some mixing.

Two structural details follow from function, and both are examined. The ventricles have thicker muscular walls than the atria because they must pump blood out of the heart rather than merely receive it, and the left ventricle is the thickest of all because it pumps blood to the entire body while the right ventricle sends it only as far as the lungs. Valves between the chambers, and at the exits, ensure the blood flows in one direction only.

Because blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle of the body — once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the rest of the body — this arrangement is called double circulation.

sections.h: Nutrition — autotrophic and heterotrophic
paras: Photosynthesis is the process by which autotrophs take in substances from outside and convert them into stored forms of energy.
bullets: The events of photosynthesis are: absorption of light energy by chlorophyll; conversion of light energy into chemical energy together with the splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen; and the reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates.
These steps need not take place one immediately after the other, and in some plants the carbon dioxide is taken up at night and used during the day.

Carbon dioxide enters through stomata, which also lose large amounts of water as vapour. The pore is bounded by two guard cells: when water flows into them they swell, the curved shape opens the pore, and when they shrink the pore closes.

Heterotrophic nutrition takes three named forms. Saprophytic organisms such as bread mould, yeast and mushrooms break down food outside the body and then absorb it. Parasites such as cuscuta, ticks, lice, leeches and tapeworms derive nutrition from a living host without killing it immediately.

Holozoic nutrition, seen in Amoeba and in humans, involves taking in whole material and then breaking it down inside the body. Amoeba engulfs food using temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia, forming a food vacuole; Paramoecium uses cilia to sweep food to a fixed spot.

sections.h: The human digestive system, gland by gland
paras: Follow the food along the alimentary canal and pair each region with the secretion that acts there — that pairing is what the marks are for.
bullets: In the mouth, saliva from the salivary glands contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which breaks down starch into sugar. The teeth crush the food and the tongue helps mix it.
The food is pushed along the oesophagus by rhythmic contractions of the muscular lining called peristaltic movements, which occur throughout the canal.

In the stomach, gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, a protein-digesting enzyme called pepsin, and mucus. The acid creates the acidic medium in which pepsin works and also kills many germs, while the mucus protects the stomach's own lining from that acid. A sphincter muscle regulates the exit of food into the small intestine.
The small intestine is the longest part of the alimentary canal and is the site of the complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

It receives bile from the liver, which makes the acidic food alkaline so that pancreatic enzymes can act, and which emulsifies fats — breaking large globules into smaller ones to increase the surface area for enzyme action.

Pancreatic juice contains trypsin for digesting proteins and lipase for breaking down emulsified fats. The intestinal juice finally converts proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates to glucose and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.
The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi, which greatly increase the surface area for absorption and are richly supplied with blood vessels.
The unabsorbed food passes into the large intestine, where villi absorb water, and the remaining material is removed through the anus, regulated by the anal sphincter.

sections.h: Respiration — three pathways from one starting point
paras: All three routes begin identically, which is the fact that makes the comparison table easy to reconstruct rather than memorise.
bullets: Glucose, a six-carbon molecule, is first broken down in the cytoplasm into a three-carbon molecule called pyruvate. This step is common to all organisms.
In the absence of oxygen, in yeast, pyruvate is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide with the release of energy. This is fermentation, and it is the basis of brewing and baking.
In our muscle cells, when oxygen supply is insufficient during sudden vigorous activity, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid. The accumulation of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.
In the presence of oxygen, in the mitochondria, pyruvate is broken down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing much more energy than either anaerobic route.
The energy released is used to make ATP, which is the energy currency of the cell; the energy is made available when ATP is broken down.
Aquatic organisms must breathe faster than terrestrial ones because the amount of dissolved oxygen in water is low compared with the oxygen available in air.

In humans, air passes through the nostrils, nasal passage, pharynx, larynx and trachea, which is supported by rings of cartilage preventing it from collapsing, then into the bronchi, bronchioles and finally the alveoli.
The alveoli are balloon-like structures providing a very large surface for gas exchange, and their walls contain an extensive network of blood vessels.
Oxygen is carried by the respiratory pigment haemoglobin present in red blood cells, while carbon dioxide, being more soluble in water, is mostly transported in the dissolved form in the plasma.

sections.h: Transportation and excretion
paras: Both systems exist because a large body cannot rely on diffusion alone.
bullets: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick elastic walls because the blood emerges under high pressure, and have no valves. Veins carry blood back to the heart, have thinner walls and possess valves that ensure blood flows only in one direction.
Capillaries have walls only one cell thick, which is what allows the exchange of materials between the blood and the surrounding cells.

Platelets circulate in the blood and plug leaks by helping the blood to clot. Lymph is a colourless fluid that carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from the tissues back into the blood.

In plants, xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves. Transpiration — the loss of water vapour from the stomata — creates a suction called transpiration pull, which draws water upward during the day; at night root pressure is the main force.

Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts, a process called translocation. Unlike transport in xylem, translocation uses energy from ATP, and material can move in either direction as required.
The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. The basic filtration unit in the kidney is the nephron.

Each nephron has a cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries called the glomerulus, associated with a cup-shaped end called Bowman's capsule. Filtration occurs here, and as the filtrate flows along the tubule, useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are selectively reabsorbed.
When the kidneys fail, the blood can be cleaned artificially by dialysis using an artificial kidney.

Plants use quite different strategies: oxygen is a waste product of photosynthesis, excess water is removed by transpiration, and other wastes are stored in cellular vacuoles, in leaves that fall off, as resins and gums in old xylem, or are excreted into the surrounding soil.

examples.t: Muscle cramp after running hard
examples.d: Sudden vigorous activity outruns the oxygen supply to the muscles, so pyruvate is converted to lactic acid instead of being fully oxidised. The accumulated lactic acid causes cramps.

examples.t: Bile contains no enzyme yet is essential for fat digestion
examples.d: Bile makes the acidic food from the stomach alkaline so pancreatic enzymes can act, and it emulsifies fats into small globules, increasing the surface area on which lipase can work.

examples.t: Villi increase surface area for absorption
examples.d: The finger-like projections lining the small intestine multiply the absorptive surface many times over and are richly supplied with blood vessels that carry the absorbed food away.

examples.t: The left ventricle has the thickest wall
examples.d: It pumps blood to the whole body, while the right ventricle sends it only to the lungs. Wall thickness follows directly from the distance the blood must be driven.

mistakes: Writing that digestion is completed in the stomach. Only protein digestion begins there; carbohydrates, proteins and fats are all completely digested in the small intestine.
Saying bile is an enzyme or that it digests fat. Bile contains no digestive enzyme — it neutralises the acid and emulsifies fat so that lipase can act.
Claiming anaerobic respiration in humans produces alcohol. Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; human muscle produces lactic acid.
Forgetting that all three respiratory pathways share the first step. Glucose is broken to pyruvate in the cytoplasm in every case; only what happens to pyruvate differs.

Stating that arteries always carry oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood back — the definition depends on direction relative to the heart, not on oxygen content.
Saying veins have thick walls to withstand pressure. It is arteries that have thick elastic walls; veins have thinner walls and valves, because blood in them is no longer under high pressure.
Confusing xylem and phloem. Xylem carries water and minerals upward and does not require energy in the same way; phloem translocates food in either direction using energy from ATP.

Describing the nephron as merely a filter. Filtration at the glomerulus is followed by selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts and much of the water as the filtrate moves along the tubule.

applications.h: Dialysis when the kidneys fail
applications.d: The nephron works by filtering the blood at the glomerulus and then selectively reabsorbing what the body needs. When kidneys stop performing this, nitrogenous wastes accumulate in the blood and become poisonous. An artificial kidney carries out haemodialysis, passing the patient's blood through tubes surrounded by a dialysing fluid that has the same osmotic composition as blood except that it contains no nitrogenous waste, so the waste diffuses out while useful substances are retained. The device is a direct engineering copy of the two-stage principle the nephron uses.

applications.h: Why athletes feel sore and why we pant after exertion
applications.d: During sudden vigorous exercise the muscles demand energy faster than oxygen can be delivered, so respiration in the muscle cells becomes anaerobic and lactic acid accumulates, producing cramps. Rapid breathing afterwards supplies the oxygen needed to deal with that accumulation. This is why gradual warming up and controlled pacing are recommended in physical training — they keep the muscles within the aerobic pathway, which also releases far more energy per glucose molecule.

applications.h: Fermentation in food and industry
applications.d: The anaerobic pathway in yeast converts pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, and both products are useful. The carbon dioxide is what makes bread dough rise, leaving the airy texture of a baked loaf, and the ethanol is the basis of brewing. The same anaerobic principle, using different microorganisms, produces curd from milk. A single step of this chapter therefore underlies a large part of traditional food processing.

applications.h: Why transpiration is not simply wasted water
applications.d: A plant loses a very large quantity of water as vapour through its stomata, which looks wasteful. But this loss creates the transpiration pull that draws water and dissolved minerals from the roots all the way up to the leaves, in tall trees against gravity and without any pump. Transpiration also helps in the regulation of temperature in the plant. Understanding this explains why plants wilt in strong sun when soil water is short, and why irrigation timing matters in agriculture.

boardQuestions.q: Describe the process of nutrition in Amoeba.
boardQuestions.a: Amoeba shows holozoic nutrition. It has a flexible cell surface and takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface called pseudopodia, which fuse over the food particle and enclose it in a food vacuole. Inside the food vacuole complex substances are broken down into simpler ones by digestive enzymes, and these diffuse into the cytoplasm where they are used for growth, maintenance and multiplication. The remaining undigested material is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out.

boardQuestions.q: What is the role of hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus in the stomach?
boardQuestions.a: Hydrochloric acid creates an acidic medium in the stomach which is necessary for the action of the enzyme pepsin, and it also kills many of the germs that enter with the food. Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme, so it begins the digestion of proteins. Mucus protects the inner lining of the stomach from the action of the hydrochloric acid, because under normal conditions the acid would otherwise damage the stomach wall itself.

boardQuestions.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration, mentioning the site, the products and the energy released.
boardQuestions.a: Both begin in the same way, with glucose, a six-carbon molecule, being broken down in the cytoplasm into a three-carbon molecule called pyruvate. In aerobic respiration the pyruvate is then broken down in the mitochondria in the presence of oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, and a large amount of energy is released. In anaerobic respiration oxygen is absent: in yeast the pyruvate is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is the process of fermentation, while in our muscle cells during sudden vigorous activity it is converted into lactic acid, whose accumulation causes cramps. Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy than aerobic respiration from the same amount of glucose. In all cases the energy released is used to make ATP, which serves as the energy currency of the cell.

boardQuestions.q: Why is double circulation necessary in human beings?
boardQuestions.a: In double circulation the blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle — once when deoxygenated blood is sent from the right side to the lungs and returns oxygenated, and again when it is pumped from the left side to the rest of the body. This is necessary because the separation of the right and left sides of the heart prevents oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing. Such separation allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen to the body, which is essential for birds and mammals because they constantly use energy to maintain their body temperature. Animals that do not maintain a constant body temperature can tolerate some mixing of the two streams.

boardQuestions.q: Draw and describe the structure of a nephron and explain how urine is formed.
boardQuestions.a: The nephron is the basic filtration unit of the kidney. Each nephron begins with a cluster of very thin-walled blood capillaries called the glomerulus, which is enclosed within a cup-shaped structure known as Bowman's capsule; this leads into a long coiled tubule that eventually opens into a collecting duct. Blood enters the glomerulus under pressure, and filtration takes place there so that water and small dissolved substances pass into Bowman's capsule while blood cells and large proteins are retained. As the filtrate flows along the tubule, substances useful to the body such as glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water are selectively reabsorbed into the surrounding blood capillaries. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much excess water there is in the body and on how much dissolved waste needs to be excreted. The fluid remaining at the end is urine, which is collected by the collecting duct and carried by the ureter to the urinary bladder for storage until it is released through the urethra.

boardQuestions.q: How are the lungs designed in human beings to maximise the area for exchange of gases?
boardQuestions.a: Within the lungs the passage divides into smaller and smaller tubes, the bronchi branching into bronchioles, which finally terminate in balloon-like structures called alveoli. The alveoli provide a very large surface for the exchange of gases, and if the surface of all the alveoli were spread out it would cover a very large area. The walls of the alveoli contain an extensive network of blood vessels, so that oxygen from the air can diffuse into the blood and carbon dioxide can diffuse out over the shortest possible distance. In addition, when we breathe out the lungs retain a residual volume of air so that there is sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and for carbon dioxide to be released.

boardQuestions.q: What are the differences between transport in xylem and in phloem?
boardQuestions.a: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves and other parts of the plant, and the movement is essentially upward. The force is provided mainly by transpiration pull, created as water evaporates from the stomata during the day, with root pressure acting mainly at night. Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis from the leaves to other parts of the plant, including storage organs such as roots, fruits and seeds, and the process is called translocation. Translocation requires energy in the form of ATP, and material can be moved in either direction according to the needs of the plant, which is not the case for xylem transport.

assertionReason.assertion: The left ventricle has thicker walls than the right ventricle.
assertionReason.reason: The left ventricle pumps blood to the entire body while the right ventricle pumps it only to the lungs.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Driving blood the far greater distance to the whole body requires greater force, which is provided by a thicker muscular wall.

assertionReason.assertion: Bile juice is essential for the digestion of fats.
assertionReason.reason: Bile juice contains the enzyme lipase, which breaks down fats.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Bile contains no enzyme; it makes the food alkaline and emulsifies fats into small globules. Lipase is present in pancreatic juice, not in bile.

assertionReason.assertion: Aquatic organisms breathe faster than terrestrial organisms.
assertionReason.reason: Fish take in oxygen through gills whereas terrestrial animals use lungs.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Which organ is used does not by itself determine the rate of breathing. The rate is higher because the amount of dissolved oxygen available in water is low compared with the oxygen available in air.

assertionReason.assertion: All arteries carry oxygenated blood.
assertionReason.reason: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart, and the pulmonary artery is the exception that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

quiz.q: The breakdown of glucose into pyruvate takes place in the:
quiz.why: Glucose is broken down into pyruvate in the cytoplasm, and this first step is common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration alike. Only the further breakdown of pyruvate in the presence of oxygen occurs in the mitochondria.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of bile?
options: Aiding the action of pancreatic enzymes
quiz.why: Bile contains no digestive enzyme, so it cannot digest proteins. It neutralises the acidic food from the stomach and emulsifies fats so that lipase from the pancreas can act on them.

quiz.q: The basic filtration unit of the kidney is the:
quiz.why: The nephron is the basic filtration unit, consisting of a glomerulus within Bowman's capsule leading into a tubule. A neuron is a nerve cell and an alveolus is a site of gas exchange in the lung.

quiz.q: In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces:
quiz.why: In the absence of oxygen yeast converts pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide with the release of energy — the process of fermentation. Lactic acid is produced in our muscle cells instead.

quiz.q: The upward movement of water in the xylem during the day is mainly due to:
quiz.why: The evaporation of water from the stomata creates transpiration pull, which draws water up the xylem during the day. Root pressure is the main force at night, and translocation is transport in the phloem.

glossary.def: The processes that together perform maintenance of the body — nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
Nutrition in which the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances, as in photosynthesis.
Nutrition in which the organism breaks down food material outside the body and then absorbs it, as in bread mould and mushrooms.
Nutrition in which whole material is taken in and then broken down inside the body, as in Amoeba and humans.
Temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface used by Amoeba to engulf food.
Rhythmic contractions of the muscles of the alimentary canal that push food forward.
The breaking of large fat globules into smaller ones by bile, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.
Finger-like projections lining the small intestine that greatly increase the surface area for absorption.
Balloon-like structures at the ends of the bronchioles that provide a large surface for gas exchange.
The respiratory pigment in red blood cells that has a high affinity for oxygen and transports it around the body.
A circulation in which the blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.
A colourless fluid that carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from tissues back into the blood.
The transport of the products of photosynthesis in the phloem, which requires energy from ATP and can occur in either direction.
The suction created by the evaporation of water from the stomata, which draws water upward through the xylem.
The basic filtration unit of the kidney, comprising a glomerulus in Bowman's capsule leading to a tubule.

revision: Four life processes: nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion. Multicellular bodies need transport because diffusion alone cannot reach interior cells.
Photosynthesis: chlorophyll absorbs light, light energy becomes chemical energy and water splits, carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrate.
Guard cells swell to open the stomatal pore and shrink to close it.
Heterotrophic types: saprophytic (mushroom), parasitic (cuscuta, tapeworm), holozoic (Amoeba, humans).
Mouth — salivary amylase on starch. Stomach — HCl, pepsin, mucus. Small intestine — bile, pancreatic juice (trypsin, lipase), intestinal juice.
Bile has no enzyme: it neutralises acid and emulsifies fat.
Digestion is COMPLETED in the small intestine; villi then absorb.
Glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm — common to all. Then: yeast → ethanol + CO₂; muscle → lactic acid; mitochondria with oxygen → CO₂ + water, far more energy.
Trachea has cartilage rings so it does not collapse; alveoli give the surface; haemoglobin carries oxygen, CO₂ travels dissolved in plasma.
Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart, thick elastic walls, no valves. Veins carry it TO the heart, thin walls, valves. The pulmonary artery is the oxygen exception.
Left ventricle is thickest — it pumps to the whole body. Blood crosses the heart twice per cycle: double circulation.
Xylem carries water up by transpiration pull; phloem translocates food both ways using ATP.
Nephron: filtration at the glomerulus, then selective reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, salts and water. Dialysis replaces it when kidneys fail.
Plant excretion: oxygen from photosynthesis, water by transpiration, wastes in vacuoles, in shed leaves, as gums and resins, or into the soil.

extraFaqs.q: Do all arteries carry oxygenated blood?
extraFaqs.a: No. An artery is defined by direction — it carries blood away from the heart — not by the oxygen content of that blood. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, and correspondingly the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium. These two vessels are the standard exceptions, and questions are often set on them precisely because the general pattern holds everywhere else.

extraFaqs.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself if it contains hydrochloric acid and a protein-digesting enzyme?
extraFaqs.a: Because the gastric glands secrete mucus alongside the acid and the enzyme. The mucus forms a protective layer over the inner lining of the stomach and prevents the hydrochloric acid from acting on the stomach wall, which is itself made of protein and would otherwise be attacked by pepsin. When this protection fails the wall is damaged, which is what happens in acidity and ulcers, so the mucus is not an incidental secretion but an essential one.

extraFaqs.q: Why is more energy released in aerobic than in anaerobic respiration?
extraFaqs.a: Both pathways begin identically, breaking glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm, so the difference lies entirely in what happens next. In anaerobic respiration the pyruvate is converted into ethanol or lactic acid, molecules that still contain a considerable amount of chemical energy that is never extracted. In aerobic respiration the pyruvate is broken down completely in the mitochondria into carbon dioxide and water, so far more of the energy stored in the original glucose molecule is released and made available as ATP.

extraFaqs.q: If transpiration loses so much water, why do plants not simply keep their stomata closed?
extraFaqs.a: Because the same pores serve two purposes. Stomata are the route by which carbon dioxide enters the leaf for photosynthesis, so keeping them shut would stop food production. The plant therefore faces a trade-off and regulates the pores through the guard cells, opening them when carbon dioxide is needed and closing them to limit water loss. The water lost is also not entirely wasted, since transpiration generates the pull that lifts water and minerals from the roots and helps regulate the plant's temperature.

class-10-social-science-federalism.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Political Science — Democratic Politics II, Federalism. It follows Power Sharing and leads into Gender, Religion and Caste.

explainers.term: What federalism is, and what it is not
paras: Federalism is a system of government in which the power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country. Usually a federation has two levels of government: one for the entire country, responsible for subjects of common national interest, and the other at the level of provinces or states, which looks after much of the day-to-day administering of the state.

The contrast is with a unitary system, where either there is only one level of government or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government. In a unitary system the central government can pass orders to the provincial or local government. In a federal system the central government cannot order the state government to do something, because the state government has powers of its own for which it is not answerable to the central government.

Notice that having states or provinces is not by itself federalism. What makes a system federal is that both levels of government are separately answerable to the people, and that neither can simply command the other in the areas assigned to it.

explainers.term: Coming together and holding together — two routes to a federation
paras: Federations are formed in two very different ways, and the difference shapes how much power the states end up with. The first route is coming together, in which independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit, so that by pooling sovereignty and retaining identity they can increase their security. The United States, Switzerland and Australia are of this kind.
In these federations all the constituent states usually have equal powers and are strong in relation to the federal government.

The second route is holding together, in which a large country decides to divide its power between the constituent states and the national government. India, Spain and Belgium are of this kind. Here the central government tends to be more powerful in relation to the states, and very often different constituent units of the federation have unequal powers — some units are granted special powers.

This distinction is what explains an apparent puzzle about India: why the Union Government is stronger than the states and why states such as Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram have special provisions. India was not assembled from previously independent states choosing to join; it was a large country distributing power downwards, and its constitutional arrangements reflect that.

sections.h: The key features of federalism
paras: Six features are given in the chapter, and questions frequently ask for any three or four of them with explanation.
bullets: There are two or more levels, or tiers, of government.
Different tiers of government govern the same citizens, but each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.
The jurisdictions of the respective levels or tiers of government are specified in the constitution, so the existence and authority of each tier is constitutionally guaranteed.
The fundamental provisions of the constitution cannot be unilaterally changed by one level of government. Such changes require the consent of both the levels of government.

Courts have the power to interpret the constitution and the powers of different levels of government. The highest court acts as an umpire if disputes arise between different levels of government in the exercise of their respective powers.
Sources of revenue for each level of government are clearly specified to ensure its financial autonomy.

The dual objectives of federalism are to safeguard and promote the unity of the country, while at the same time accommodating regional diversity. Two aspects are crucial for its success: mutual trust between the levels of government, and agreement to live together.

sections.h: How the Constitution divides powers in India
paras: The Constitution originally provided for a two-tier system of government, the Union Government and the State Governments, and later a third tier was added. It declared India a Union of States, and specified a three-fold distribution of legislative powers.
bullets: The Union List includes subjects of national importance such as defence of the country, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency. It contains 97 subjects. They are included in this list because a uniform policy on these matters is needed throughout the country, and only the Union Government can make laws relating to them.

The State List contains subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation, comprising 66 subjects. The State Governments alone can make laws relating to them.

The Concurrent List includes subjects of common interest to both the Union Government and the State Governments, such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession, comprising 47 subjects. Both can make laws on these subjects, and if their laws conflict, the law made by the Union Government prevails.

Subjects that do not fall in any of the three lists are called residuary subjects — computer software is the example given, since the makers of the Constitution could not have anticipated it. The Union Government has the power to legislate on these.

Not all states in the Indian Union have identical powers. Some enjoy a special status: Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram have special provisions owing to their peculiar social and historical circumstances.

There are also units of the Indian Union that enjoy very little power. These are areas too small to become an independent State but which could not be merged with any existing State, and they are called Union Territories, where the Central Government has special powers.

The sharing of power between the Union and the States is basic to the structure of the Constitution, and Parliament cannot change this arrangement on its own. Any such change has first to be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority, and then has to be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states.

In case of any dispute about the division of powers, the High Courts and the Supreme Court make a decision. Both levels of government also have the power to raise resources by levying taxes, which secures their financial autonomy.

sections.h: How federalism is practised — language and Centre–State relations
paras: The chapter's most important argument is that the real success of federalism in India lies not only in the constitutional provisions but in the nature of democratic politics that has followed them.
bullets: The creation of linguistic States was the first and a major test for democratic politics in our country. Between 1947 and now several old States vanished and new ones were created, and boundaries were changed to create States where people speaking the same language lived in the same State.

Some States were created not on the basis of language but to recognise differences based on culture, ethnicity or geography — Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Telangana are of this kind.
At first many feared that creating States on the basis of language would lead to the disintegration of the country. Instead it has made the country more united and has made administration easier.

On language policy, the Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, but Hindi is the mother tongue of only about forty per cent of Indians, so there were provisions to protect other languages. Besides Hindi, there are 22 languages recognised as Scheduled Languages by the Constitution.

The use of English for official purposes was to have stopped in 1965. Many non-Hindi speaking States demanded that its use continue, and in Tamil Nadu this movement took a violent form. The Central Government responded by agreeing to continue the use of English along with Hindi for official purposes.

On Centre–State relations, for a long time the same party ruled both at the Centre and in most of the States, and the Central Government would often misuse the Constitution to dismiss State governments controlled by rival parties, undermining the spirit of federalism.

This changed after 1989 with the rise of regional political parties and the era of coalition governments at the Centre, which led to a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of State Governments. A Supreme Court judgment also made it difficult for the Central Government to dismiss State governments in an arbitrary manner.

sections.h: Decentralisation and the third tier
paras: When power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to local government, it is called decentralisation.
bullets: The basic idea is that a large number of problems and issues are best settled at the local level, because people have a better knowledge of problems in their localities and better ideas about where to spend money and how to manage things more efficiently. It also allows people to participate directly in decision making.
A major step was taken in 1992, when the Constitution was amended to make the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective.
It is now constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections to local government bodies.
Seats are reserved in the elected bodies and in the executive heads of these institutions for the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.
At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women.
An independent State Election Commission has been created in each State to conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
The State governments are required to share some powers and revenue with local government bodies, though the nature of sharing varies from State to State.

In rural areas the local government is called panchayati raj. The gram panchayat is the decision-making body for the whole village, with ward members called panch and a president or sarpanch, directly elected by the adult population of the village.

The gram panchayat works under the overall supervision of the gram sabha, of which all the voters in the village are members. It meets at least twice or thrice a year to approve the annual budget of the gram panchayat and to review its performance.

A few gram panchayats are grouped together to form a panchayat samiti or block or mandal, and all the panchayat samitis or mandals in a district together constitute the zilla parishad, whose chairperson is its political head.

In urban areas, municipalities are set up in towns and municipal corporations in big cities. The political head of a municipality is the municipal chairperson, and in a municipal corporation the corresponding officer is called the mayor.

examples.t: Belgium moved from unitary to federal
examples.d: Belgium changed its constitution in 1993 to shift from a unitary to a federal system, showing that a country can accommodate diversity by redistributing power rather than by breaking apart.

examples.t: Computer software as a residuary subject
examples.d: It appears on none of the three lists because the makers of the Constitution could not have foreseen it. Residuary subjects fall to the Union Government.

examples.t: English retained alongside Hindi after 1965
examples.d: Use of English for official purposes was to end in 1965, but non-Hindi States objected, with violent protest in Tamil Nadu, and the Central Government agreed to continue it — federalism working through negotiation.

examples.t: The gram sabha supervises the gram panchayat
examples.d: All voters of the village are members of the gram sabha, which meets two or three times a year to approve the budget and review performance — direct democracy checking the elected body.

mistakes: Confusing federal with unitary. In a unitary system the central government can order the sub-units; in a federal system it cannot, because each level has its own constitutionally guaranteed jurisdiction.

Saying Hindi is the national language of India. The Constitution did not give the status of national language to any language; Hindi is the official language, and 22 languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages.
Placing education or forests in the State List. Both are on the Concurrent List, where the Union and the States can both legislate and the Union law prevails in case of conflict.
Assuming residuary subjects go to the States. They fall to the Union Government, which is one of the features making the Indian federation a holding-together type with a stronger centre.
Writing that all Indian States have identical powers. Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram have special provisions, and Union Territories have far less power than States.
Claiming Parliament can change the division of powers by itself. Any change requires a two-thirds majority in both Houses and then ratification by the legislatures of at least half the States.

Treating decentralisation as the same thing as federalism. Federalism is the division between the Union and the States; decentralisation is the further transfer of power to a third tier of local government, given constitutional force by the amendment of 1992.
Confusing the gram sabha with the gram panchayat. The panchayat is the elected decision-making body; the gram sabha is the body of all voters that supervises it.

applications.h: Why linguistic reorganisation strengthened rather than broke the country
applications.d: When States were reorganised so that people speaking the same language lived in the same State, many feared it would encourage separatism and lead to the disintegration of India. The opposite happened. Recognising the claim to linguistic identity removed a major grievance, made administration easier because government could be conducted in a language people actually spoke, and left regional identity with no reason to become a demand for separation. This is the clearest practical demonstration of federalism's dual objective — accommodating diversity in order to preserve unity.

applications.h: Coalition politics as a check on the Centre
applications.d: The constitutional provisions on Centre–State relations did not change after 1989, yet the practice changed a great deal. When a single party held power at the Centre and in most States, the Union Government often dismissed State governments run by rivals. The rise of regional parties and the necessity of coalition governments meant the Centre depended on regional allies and could no longer act so freely, and a Supreme Court judgment made arbitrary dismissal difficult. The lesson is that federalism depends on the nature of democratic politics as much as on the written text.

applications.h: Reservation of one-third of local seats for women
applications.d: The 1992 amendment made it mandatory to reserve at least one-third of all positions in local bodies for women, along with reservations for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes. As a result more than ten lakh elected women representatives entered local government. This is decentralisation used deliberately as an instrument of social change: it brought into public decision making a group that had been largely absent from it, at the level closest to everyday life.

applications.h: Why local problems are best solved locally
applications.d: A State government sitting in a distant capital cannot know which village handpump has failed, which stretch of road floods, or where a school building is unsafe. People living in the locality have that knowledge and a direct interest in acting on it. Decentralisation therefore improves both the accuracy of decisions and the speed with which they are taken, and it gives ordinary citizens a realistic opportunity to participate directly rather than only through a vote once in five years.

boardQuestions.q: What is federalism? State any four key features of a federal system of government.
boardQuestions.a: Federalism is a system of government in which the power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country, usually with one government for the entire country and another at the level of provinces or states. Among its key features, first, there are two or more levels or tiers of government. Second, different tiers of government govern the same citizens, but each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration. Third, the jurisdictions of the respective levels are specified in the constitution, so the existence and authority of each tier is constitutionally guaranteed. Fourth, the fundamental provisions of the constitution cannot be unilaterally changed by one level of government, as such changes require the consent of both levels. In addition, courts have the power to interpret the constitution and act as an umpire in disputes between the levels, and the sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified to ensure financial autonomy.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between coming together and holding together federations with examples.
boardQuestions.a: In a coming together federation, independent states come together on their own to form a bigger unit, so that by pooling sovereignty and retaining identity they can increase their security. The United States, Switzerland and Australia are examples. In such federations all the constituent states usually have equal powers and are strong in relation to the federal government. In a holding together federation, a large country decides to divide its power between the constituent states and the national government, as in India, Spain and Belgium. Here the central government tends to be more powerful in relation to the states, and very often different constituent units are given unequal powers, with some units granted special status. India is a holding together federation, which is why the Union Government is comparatively stronger and why States such as Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram enjoy special provisions.

boardQuestions.q: Describe the three-fold distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the State Governments in India.
boardQuestions.a: The Constitution provides three lists. The Union List includes subjects of national importance such as defence of the country, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency, and contains 97 subjects; these are placed here because a uniform policy is needed throughout the country, and only the Union Government can make laws on them. The State List contains subjects of state and local importance such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation, comprising 66 subjects, on which only the State Governments can make laws. The Concurrent List contains subjects of common interest to both, such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession, comprising 47 subjects; both governments can make laws on these, but if their laws conflict, the law made by the Union Government prevails. Subjects that do not fall in any of these lists, such as computer software, are called residuary subjects, and the Union Government has the power to legislate on them.

boardQuestions.q: How has the practice of federalism in India been strengthened since 1989?
boardQuestions.a: For a long time the same party ruled both at the Centre and in most of the States, and the Central Government often misused the Constitution to dismiss State governments that were controlled by rival parties, which went against the spirit of federalism. After 1989 there was a rise of regional political parties and the beginning of an era of coalition governments at the Centre, so that the leading national party had to enter into alliances with regional parties and could no longer disregard their interests. Around the same time a Supreme Court judgment made it difficult for the Central Government to dismiss State governments in an arbitrary manner. Together these developments led to a new culture of power sharing and greater respect for the autonomy of State Governments.

boardQuestions.q: What is decentralisation? Describe the main provisions of the constitutional amendment of 1992 relating to local government.
boardQuestions.a: When power is taken away from Central and State governments and given to local government, it is called decentralisation. The basic idea is that a large number of problems and issues are best settled at the local level, since people have a better knowledge of problems in their localities and can participate directly in decision making. In 1992 the Constitution was amended to make the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective. It became constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections to local government bodies. Seats were reserved in the elected bodies and in the executive heads of these institutions for the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes. At least one-third of all positions were reserved for women. An independent State Election Commission was created in each State to conduct panchayat and municipal elections. Finally, the State governments were required to share some powers and revenue with local government bodies, though the nature of this sharing varies from State to State.

boardQuestions.q: Explain India's language policy and how it helped avoid conflict.
boardQuestions.a: The Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, but since Hindi is the mother tongue of only about forty per cent of Indians there were provisions to protect other languages, and 22 languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages by the Constitution. A candidate in an examination conducted for the Central Government positions may opt to take the examination in any of these languages. The use of English for official purposes was to have stopped in 1965, but many non-Hindi speaking States demanded that its use continue, and in Tamil Nadu the movement took a violent form. The Central Government responded by agreeing to continue the use of English along with Hindi for official purposes. This flexibility, and the willingness to accommodate the claims of non-Hindi speakers rather than impose Hindi, is why India avoided the kind of language conflict that troubled Sri Lanka.

assertionReason.assertion: India is described as a holding together federation.
assertionReason.reason: A large country divided its power between the constituent states and the national government rather than independent states coming together.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. India was not assembled from previously independent states pooling sovereignty; power was distributed downwards, which is the defining feature of a holding together federation.

assertionReason.assertion: Parliament cannot on its own change the sharing of power between the Union and the States.
assertionReason.reason: The Constitution describes India as a Union of States.
assertionReason.why: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. The description of India as a Union of States is a matter of naming. The protection comes from the amendment procedure: such a change must be passed by both Houses with a two-thirds majority and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half the States.

assertionReason.assertion: Hindi is the national language of India.
assertionReason.reason: Hindi is the mother tongue of about forty per cent of Indians.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true. The Constitution did not give the status of national language to any language; Hindi is the official language, and the fact that it is spoken by only about forty per cent is exactly why other languages were protected.

assertionReason.assertion: The creation of linguistic States strengthened the unity of India.
assertionReason.reason: Every State in India was created solely on the basis of language.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Reorganisation on linguistic lines did make the country more united and administration easier, but several States were created to recognise differences of culture, ethnicity or geography rather than language — Nagaland, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Telangana among them.

extraFaqs.q: Is having states enough to make a country federal?
extraFaqs.a: No. What matters is whether the sub-units have powers of their own that the central government cannot simply override. In a unitary system a country may well be divided into provinces or states, but the central government can pass orders to them and they are answerable to it. In a federal system each level has a jurisdiction specified in the constitution, both levels are separately answerable to the people, and neither can unilaterally change the fundamental division of powers. It is that constitutional guarantee, not the existence of states, that makes a system federal.

extraFaqs.q: Why is India's central government stronger than that of the United States?
extraFaqs.a: Because the two federations were formed by different routes. The United States is a coming together federation, in which previously independent states pooled their sovereignty voluntarily and therefore retained substantial power, with all constituent states holding equal powers. India is a holding together federation, in which a large country divided its power downwards to its constituent states. In such federations the central government tends to be more powerful, and different units may be given unequal powers — which is why some Indian States have special provisions and why Union Territories have very limited powers.

extraFaqs.q: What happens when a Union law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject conflict?
extraFaqs.a: The law made by the Union Government prevails. Both the Union and the State Governments are entitled to make laws on the 47 subjects of the Concurrent List, such as education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession, because these are matters of common interest. But if their laws conflict with each other on the same subject, the Constitution resolves it in favour of the Union law. If a dispute arises over whether a subject falls within a particular level's jurisdiction, the High Courts and the Supreme Court decide.

extraFaqs.q: Why did the Constitution not make Hindi the national language?
extraFaqs.a: Because Hindi is the mother tongue of only about forty per cent of Indians, so declaring it the national language would have imposed the language of a minority of the population on everyone else. The makers of the Constitution instead identified Hindi as the official language and included provisions to protect other languages, recognising 22 languages as Scheduled Languages. The wisdom of this caution was shown when the planned discontinuation of English in 1965 provoked strong opposition from non-Hindi speaking States, and the Central Government's willingness to continue English alongside Hindi defused a conflict that had torn other countries apart.
